title: AMA | November 2026
transcriptText:
0:00:00.3 Sean Carroll: Hello everyone, and welcome to the November 2026 Ask Me Anything edition of the Mindscape Podcast. I'm your host, Sean Carroll. As you're listening to this, we have had an election in the United States, November 2026, a midterm election. The questions in this month's AMA don't involve that election, mostly because they came in before the election happened, but I'm recording it after the election happened. For those of you 500 years from now who don't know what we're talking about, the Democratic Party, which was not in power, gained a huge amount of power. In particular, they won majorities in both the Senate and the House of Representatives in Congress. Still don't have the presidency, of course; there was not a presidential election. Still don't have the Supreme Court. Supreme Court is supposed to be completely apolitical, but that is hilariously untrue. The Supreme Court is very political and very much on the conservative side these days. But they did, the Democrats, gain both houses of Congress.
0:00:57.0 SC: We're not gonna go into details about the election results, except to mention a structural feature that is kind of amusing. This election had a couple of very explicit examples of what is known as a dummymander. Again, for those of you who aren't following US politics or don't know how things work, there's this idea called a gerrymander, which is when you have certain conditions in place, namely number one, you have winner-take-all voting system. First-past-the-post, it's sometimes called. So in any one geographic district, or any one district in general, whoever just gets the most votes wins. Secondly, you have geographic districts, so you have boundaries drawn in literal two-dimensional maps that determine what district is being represented by somebody. And then third, you have the ability to draw these maps put in the hands of perhaps partisan governments. So if you're already in the majority, if you're in control of some state, you can under certain circumstances draw the maps however you want to decide what counts as a certain congressional district.
0:02:10.3 SC: All of these features, majority vote, geographic districts, putting the drawing of the districts in the hands of a perhaps partisan majority, are bad. They're not good features of a working government, but some of these things get in there, and once they're in there, they're very hard to get rid of. So we have all these in many places in the United States, and that opens the door to what is called gerrymandering. We actually talked about gerrymandering here on the podcast from a mathematical point of view with Jordan Ellenberg quite a while ago. How well can you do it? How can you avoid doing it? How can you look at a map and know whether or not it's been gerrymandered or not?
0:02:48.0 SC: So the idea of gerrymandering is the following. Imagine you have some number of districts, 10 districts in a state, and imagine that 50% of the voters typically are one party and 50% are the other. You'd expect that on average, of those 10 districts, five of them would end up being represented by one party and the other five by the other party. But what you can do is you can use the kind of detailed demographic information that people now have to carefully draw the districts so that the party that is not in power gets put in a small number of districts where almost all their voters are. So you could have, you know, two districts with a huge number of Party A, and then eight districts with a small majority for Party B. So that even though in population terms it's 50-50 Party A, Party B, in majority in the district terms, Party B is now way ahead. Okay, that's a gerrymander, because these districts that end up doing that end up looking very complicated. And Elbridge Gerry was the politician who became notable for doing it, and one of the districts that he drew, or I forget whether he was the one who drew them or was voted into it, but it sort of looked like a salamander in the eyes of a political cartoonist.
0:04:07.3 SC: Anyway, the dummymander is people aren't actually stuck forever voting for one party or the other. They can change their minds. And in a midterm election, which is very often pushing against the party in power, people just don't like the party in power. That's a very standard feature of democracies. So it can be the case that even though overall, usually on average it's 50-50, maybe in this election, there's a strong majority of people voting for Party A over Party B. And what you've done is arrange it so that your party has a majority usually in most districts, but that majority is small. So if there's sort of a wave election that pushes many people to the other party, suddenly you can actually have fewer seats than you think you deserved, because in the districts that you tried to make 60-40, they're actually majority the other way. This is called the dummymander.
0:05:14.2 SC: And there's evidence that precisely this happened in various cases in this year's election, which, of course, is bringing some guilty pleasure to the party that benefits from this, some sadness to the party that loses. But it's certainly an advertisement for trying to do better when organizing your political system so that things like this should just never happen in the first place. And that's where I come out here.
0:05:39.8 SC: Anyway, we're not talking about that during the AMA, but I thought it was something to bring up because we're still very much in the period of time where we're dealing with the implications of these new election results, pro and con, people reacting in different ways. It's kind of amusing from a spectator's point of view. Thanks as always to the folks who support these Ask Me Anything episodes. Those are the folks who pledge on Patreon. That could be you. You could go to patreon.com/seanmcarroll. And these days we've switched over Patreon's way of paying things, so you pay by the month, not by the episode, but it's essentially the same thing. And if you think you get a dollar or two of pleasure or reward from a typical Mindscape episode, we would love it if you pledged that much support. And as a benefit, you get ad-free versions of the podcast. Unless you like the ads—you're still allowed to listen to the ads, I suppose. And you also get the right to ask these Ask Me Anything questions.
0:06:43.7 SC: So all the questions you're about to hear come from Patreon supporters who we greatly appreciate for their support. And with that, let's go. Peter says, "If you could have a superpower, what would it be? Flight, super strength, super speed, teleportation, telekinesis, et cetera." Classic question. Mostly a classic question when you're 15 years old. But that's okay. We all have the inner 15-year-old who really cares about these things. My standard answer would be teleportation. Teleportation. But this is an old person's answer. Okay? It's just a pain to have to travel in these awkward ways. Just last week, as I'm recording this, I zipped down very quickly to Santa Fe to visit the Santa Fe Institute, where we were having a small workshop on timelessness. At SFI, I have been serving on a small committee that's been organizing a series of events about time and the arrow of time and things like that. And this was sort of the last event in that series that's been going on for years.
0:07:52.1 SC: And so I felt I had to go. I had an obligation to go. Of course, it's fun to go. I don't really have time to go, but it was on timelessness, which is a certain delicious irony. So I went. And the point of it is, I was trying very hard to get there in a hurry to sort of miss the fewest classes that I'm supposed to be teaching while also making it for as much of the meeting as I could. And I came very, very close to missing a connection while I was flying out there. In fact, I came very close to missing connections both ways, flying out there and flying back, because I was flying directly to Santa Fe. Sorry, the word directly is wrong there. I was flying to Santa Fe rather than to Albuquerque, which is where I usually go. Usually you go to Albuquerque, rent a car, drive an hour to Santa Fe. That's perfectly convenient. And there's a lot more flights to Albuquerque than there are to the tiny little Santa Fe airport. But I wanted to get there in a hurry, so I flew to Santa Fe, which means there's no direct flights from Baltimore. And what that meant was that I was sitting in O'Hare working on my talk, as one does, and they switched the gate on me. And I never noticed until very late.
0:09:04.1 SC: Anyway, I did notice in time. So I got to the correct gate, which is in a completely different, not terminal, but region of the terminal. And so that was a close call. And again, irony, because I was going to a workshop on timelessness and the existence of time was very important. And then likewise, when I came back, there was rain or snow or something. It couldn't have been snow. It must have been rain and fog in Denver, which delayed my flight into Denver, but not my flight out. So once again, I came very close to missing that. So anyway, the point is, with teleportation, presumably, I'd be able to avoid all that, right? I could just walk out the door and be in Santa Fe instantly later. Now, there's practicalities. If I was the only person in the world who could do teleportation, then are you sure when you teleport somewhere that you know exactly where you're teleporting to and that there's not a person standing there and you land inside their body and explode or something like that? I think you'd have to work out a lot of the practicalities there. So maybe teleportation is less good than it seems. But if everyone could teleport, I mean, the world would be a very bad, messy place, I think. That would be good in some ways, but bad in other ways. So maybe I should grow out of my thought that having teleportation ability would be the best.
0:10:24.3 SC: Again, since I'm an old person now, I don't know if it's a superpower, but health would be a wonderful... My health is fine right now, but it doesn't last forever. And if you had these healing factors like Wolverine has, and you could just get better... I don't know, does that work for a stomach flu and things like that? I don't know. It works when you're stabbed, but I don't know what the general theory of the healing factor would be. But to bounce back from small indignities in your body would be very, very useful right now. I think, honestly, thinking about telepathy and things like that, seeing into other people's minds, I don't want anyone to see into my mind and I don't want to see into anyone else's. I think that talking is a perfectly good way of doing things. Flying was... Maybe flying is the compromise. If you could fly very quickly, I think once again, there's practicalities. It gets cold up there and there's a lot of drones flying around in the atmosphere these days. So if you had flying without the ability to heal, you might bump into a drone and hurt yourself very badly. So this superpower thing, it's less good than the comic books make it out to be. There's all sorts of things, higher order questions you need to take into account.
0:11:41.6 SC: James McBeath said, "In the September 2026 AMA, you said the eternal Schwarzschild solution..." That's the solution to Einstein's equations in general relativity for a spherically symmetric empty space distribution. "Anyway, the eternal Schwarzschild solution has all sorts of weird properties. It has not only a black hole, but has a white hole in the past out of which things can come but nothing can go in. But the Einstein-Rosen bridge and the white hole are not really thought to exist in the world. But we study them because there's a simple mathematical setup to look at first."
0:12:12.8 SC: And then James continues, "In other podcasts, you said that scientists should have the courage to accept what the math is telling them. How do you decide when to accept the math and when to assume the predictions don't really exist?" It's an excellent question and it points to a little bit of sloppiness on my part in saying things like you should accept the math. The important thing is you should accept the math... You should never accept the math in the sense that you just believe it no matter what. What I think is that you should take seriously what the math about your theory is trying to tell you to the extent that you think your theory is right and you've set up the mathematical formulation of the problem correctly. So in the case of the eternal Schwarzschild black hole, the math isn't telling you that the eternal Schwarzschild black hole exists. The eternal Schwarzschild black hole is a mathematical solution to Einstein's equation in an otherwise entirely empty universe. But we don't live in an otherwise entirely empty universe.
0:13:18.2 SC: The black holes that we care about in our universe are created from stars, right? Stars collapsing or other things that are analogous to stars. So the point is that there are absolutely black hole solutions that are relevant in the real world, but they're solutions that don't start with a white hole. They start with a star or some collection of matter and then the black hole develops over time. So the eternal Schwarzschild black hole is a mathematical solution, but not one of any physical relevance. And it's not a matter of not having the courage to accept it. It's just not an expression of the physical situation we care about. That's in contrast to the very existence of black holes, which was kind of implicit in Schwarzschild's original solution in 1917. And no one believed it. No one really paid attention. No one even figured out what it was trying to say until the 1950s and people like David Finkelstein.
0:14:15.1 SC: And also things like the Big Bang. Oh, there's a singularity at the beginning of the universe. Things like the multiverse, if you believe in Many-Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics. Now, all of these are cases where physically realistic initial setups imply that the equations are telling you something dramatic. So there you either need to have the courage to accept what the math is telling you or you change the math. You change the theory, you believe in a different kind of theory, and that's also fine. I'm not against changing the theory if the theory doesn't seem to be leading you where you want it to. What I'm against is having a theory that you accept, having a well-formulated idea of what initial conditions are and what solutions should be relevant, and then just not choosing... Choosing not to quite accept the implications of your theory given those conditions. That's not what's going on with the eternal Schwarzschild black hole and its wormhole.
0:15:13.8 SC: Friedrich says, "As a European, I regularly have to watch with horror how the American election system creates really poor outcomes for everyone involved. But from a physics of democracy perspective, aren't you stuck somehow? The politicians who would change anything are the ones who are heavily dependent on its existence. And psychologically, most voters can probably not fathom any alternative without having lived abroad for some time. Do you see a path that would work to move to enable better outcomes without destabilizing society on a catastrophic level?" I think this is a super good question. I think it's more just a democracy question and an institutional structure question than a physics of democracy question, but still an excellent question. If I can just rephrase it in much more general terms, we had a period here in the United States 250 years ago where we were thinking about how to structure the government. This is something actually in the book, The Physics of Democracy, that I'm supposed to be working on. I mention this as a contrast.
0:16:14.4 SC: Between physics notions of emergence and coarse graining versus political notions of emergence and coarse graining. So part of the book is saying that certain analogies or metaphors are useful. They shed light, they illuminate on what's going on in political situations. But also I try to say, okay, the following things don't work. I have a little screed in there why quantum mechanics is really not relevant to political or social situations at all. And the story of emergence and taking individuals in a large number and having them collectively work to get some goal or something like that is very similar in politics and physics. But there are important differences. And the most important difference is in physics, the correct way to coarse grain, that is to say, the particular ways in which you throw out some microscopic information to keep certain macroscopic variables, is fixed by the physical situation. It's fixed by the demand that you get a predictive theory that uses only the macroscopic variables that you've coarse grained away from the microscopic variables.
0:17:31.2 SC: In politics, you're not interested in a predictive theory. I mean, maybe you want a predictive theory of politics, that's fine. But when you're inventing a voting or representation system, the goal, the standard of success, is correctly representing the will of the people, whatever that means. And you have to decide what mechanism it is to do that. And the ability to predict the future is just not a standard for that, for the success of representing what the people want. So 250 years ago, people were debating this, and it was an interesting kind of discussion because democracy theory was still relatively primitive and young compared to where it is now. The United States in its current system of government is actually old compared to many other current systems of governments in other countries. And so they made some choices, and some choices they made were good. And some choices they made were bad.
0:18:29.4 SC: Overall, the people, though, were a fairly impressive group of people. And they were fairly thoughtful. And of course they disagreed with each other about important things, but they were trying their best to do a good job, I think. And now, as Friedrich points out, there are problems. So one issue is just this issue of winner-take-all, majority rule, right? It's a little bit different. So there's sort of two things. One is your voting system, which is to say, how do you pick the representative? But then there's also your representation system, which is what is the set of representatives that you're picking? I think to Americans, the idea that you have a geographically chosen district, like you draw a line on a map and inside is your district and outside is everything else, and one person represents that district, that's almost baked in. They don't even imagine there could be a difference from that system to something else.
0:19:32.0 SC: So they will examine ways of choosing those representatives with different voting systems. It doesn't need to be plurality votes or majority votes. It could be ranked choice voting or approval voting or there's other systems that are interesting there, but the idea that there should be a representative for a district is kind of seen as self-evident to a lot of Americans. It's not self-evident. You can do other things. You can do systems of proportional representation. If you have 60% of the people in one district members of one political party and 40% members of another one, you could have 10 representatives for that area. Maybe the area is 10 times as big as a typical US district. But okay, we can debate that. But you could have 10 people represent, and then you could have situations where rather than voting for individuals, the voters vote for a party. And if the party gets 60% of the votes in a 10-representative district, they get to pick six representatives, and the 40% party gets to pick four.
0:20:36.9 SC: Now, Americans don't like that. You tell them that, you even suggest it, and they kind of recoil, in part because they don't like political parties. And that's in part because political parties are kind of decorative in some sense in the United States. I mean, we have political parties, we split up into them, but the party apparatuses typically don't have the level of power and decision-making that they do in parliamentary systems.
0:21:00.1 SC: So anyway, this is all to say there are alternative systems, like Friedrich mentions. Many European countries use various kinds of alternative systems. These alternative systems, by the way, have their own issues. Because when you have a system, for example, like proportional representation, then, okay, what if you don't have two parties? What if you have more than two parties? It's still very possible for people to be not represented effectively, and there's different sorts of dynamics going on that get in the way. But I think... Sorry, I'm just sort of talking around the problem. The actual question Friedrich is asking is effectively, could it get changed? Could you imagine, I don't know whether for some questions you'd have to amend the Constitution to the US, for other questions you could do it just through the ordinary legislative process, but could you implement a better system?
0:21:56.3 SC: And actually, I kind of very much feel the worry that Friedrich is implying here, that I kind of don't want to upset the applecart too much because I don't have trust that the people who would do the redesign would be as smart and as civically minded as the people who did the designing 250 years ago. I do think there's no question in my mind that there are absolutely better systems than the United States has. And I don't know what the perfect system is, but in many ways, the one that we have here is obviously bad and could be improved. Do I have the faith or trust that the people in power now would effectively improve it? No, I do not. Do I have the trust that there is any mechanism that could choose people to be put in charge and, let's say, have a new Constitutional Convention that would completely from scratch rewrite the Constitution of the United States? Oh my God, no. That's a very, very frightening prospect to me. I just don't think that the people who would be chosen for that would be good people.
0:23:03.6 SC: It could be. It's possible to imagine good people really, really improving the governmental system of the United States. And by good, I don't mean on my side of the political divides. I just mean smart people who know about politics and who are motivated by what's best for the country, not what's best for their particular partisan side. I'm just not sure how we would ever make that happen. So I think that the fact that the United States Constitution allows for itself to be amended, but that amending it is difficult, I think that was a smart move on the part of the authors of the Constitution. You should be able to fix it, but it should be hard to fix it because it's too easy to break it. And even though it's clear that it could be improved, not changing it is better than making it dramatically, dramatically worse. So maybe I'm being too pessimistic there. I don't know what the real political scientists would think of that. I would love it if we had a slightly more sensible political system.
0:24:01.2 SC: Lucas Pollard says, "Have you ever significantly changed your mind about a scientific or philosophical question without encountering new evidence, simply because you came to understand the existing arguments differently?" Sure, yeah, all the time. I mean, I'm not even quite sure how to come up with an example for that, but I mean, I think it's absolutely true that as one thinks about things, one can change one's mind. In fact, I do think I'm not gonna be very good at giving you examples just because there are too many. I mean, maybe moral objectivity is an example for me. Like, I used to think years ago that you could be scientific about morality and derive principles of morality roughly based on the idea that we had evolved through natural selection to survive, and the things that would make us survive and flourish can be mapped onto moral principles.
0:24:55.0 SC: Now, just by thinking about it, and more data came in, but just by thinking about it, reading and listening to other people, I understand that that was wishful thinking. That, of course, we do evolve through natural selection, and from that we get preferences and intuitions and inclinations, but those are not morally objective facts, suppose I should say objective moral facts. They are the instincts that we get from natural selection. Those are different than what our moral principles should be. So now I'm not a moral realist anymore. But I think that more generally, there's an interesting question here about what it means to be a good Bayesian. We often mention being a good Bayesian here on Mindscape, and we cast it in terms of: you have credences over a set of propositions, and new information comes in, new data, and you update your credences based on the likelihood of getting that data.
0:25:51.4 SC: Of course, new ideas or new thoughts should count as new data. But do they count as new, how do we count them as new data? This is an excellent question that I don't know the answer to. I almost said the answer is not known, but probably someone knows the answer, or at least people have very well-thought-out opinions about these things. I am not up on the best writings or thinkings about these exact issues. In fact, now that I'm thinking about it, I have a better example. A classic example is, believe it or not, the electroweak theory. Steven Weinberg, in, I don't know, 1967, I think it was, wrote his famous paper, "A Theory of Leptons," where he showed how you could unify electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force. And no one paid any attention. It was a very short paper, appeared in Physical Review Letters. Weinberg himself didn't pay... He never sort of cited his own paper in the papers that he wrote in the years after that. And we know why. Well, we know part of the reason why.
0:26:55.5 SC: One reason why is just it was a speculative idea. But another reason why is there was a theoretical argument that said it can't work, namely that the theory seemed to be non-renormalizable, which is another way of saying that if you did calculations, you would get infinities that you can't get rid of. So it didn't seem to be physically plausible or physically promising. And then it was approximately 1972 that Gerard 't Hooft, and in part in collaboration with Tini Veltman, showed that theories of that form, with a Higgs mechanism and spontaneous symmetry breaking and things like that, are renormalizable after all. And then suddenly it became hugely popular. So five years later, it went from no one paying attention to hugely popular. No new data had appeared. All that had appeared was an improved understanding of what the theory was really about. So things like that happen all the time in science, not to mention in philosophy. And so that's an example where it's not just me changing my mind, it's the community as a whole.
0:28:01.9 SC: Rue Phillips says, "I love the recent episode with Greg Caruso. I know you're not a fan of free will discussions, but keep them coming. I'm curious how you would compare and contrast your compatibilist views with Greg's free will skeptic views, specifically on what changes to the US legal system should theoretically be pursued. I'm having a hard time understanding the differences between compatibilists and skeptics like Greg, and I'm hoping that when I should..." Sorry, I read that without the correct pausing. "I'm having a hard time understanding the differences between compatibilists and skeptics like Greg. And I'm hoping that when applied to a specific case, like how we might modify the justice system, might make it a little more clear."
0:28:39.6 SC: Yeah, unfortunately, or for the question, but not unfortunately for the world, I don't think there is much of a difference. I think what came out in that discussion, and by the way, no free will discussions coming up anytime soon. I did Christian List and that was enough for a year, but he was on one side and I thought it was fair to have someone from the other side. And Greg is a very well-spoken and well-known articulator of the other view. So we did both of those. That's enough for a while. We can cleanse our palates now and not have more free will discussions. But I think that what came out from talking to Greg was his motivation for declining the offer to use free will vocabulary to discuss human beings making choices, which he admits human beings make choices even though they're completely physical creatures. He just doesn't want to call it free will. Why not? Well, because to him, calling it free will implies this kind of moral desert. It implies a kind of way of thinking about human beings where if you make the wrong choices, you are bad and you deserve to be punished.
0:29:51.8 SC: To me, that just doesn't follow at all. That's a separate thing. Okay. I can absolutely imagine applying the vocabulary of human beings thinking things through and making choices, making the wrong choices, or bad or evil choices, whatever you want to call them, and dealing with them in ways that do not simply involve punishing them because they're bad. That just is a non sequitur. They're separate questions. One is the question of how we analyze and talk about human behavior. The other is how we organize the justice system and our ideas of what people deserve and things like that. So I don't see any real difference. As a compatibilist, I'm completely happy with a point of view that says we should try to, number one, rehabilitate people who have behaved badly. Number two, deter them from doing further bad things. And those should be the central focuses of the justice system, not punishing people because they are bad.
0:30:56.0 SC: Jeffrey Siegel says, "I was wondering whether you think it is just as well that there does not seem to be the possibility of faster-than-light travel or communication. As I think von Neumann pointed out, since our species has evolved rather late in the development of the universe, if faster-than-light travel were possible, it's likely that a species that developed earlier might have already spread through the galaxy, including Earth, and blocked the evolution of humans. Similarly, with faster-than-light communication, a more advanced civilization might be able to hack our technology and doom humanity. Given those possible dangers, do you nevertheless hope that faster-than-light travel or communication may be possible, or do you breathe a sigh of relief that it is not?"
0:31:35.4 SC: So I think I wouldn't exactly characterize von Neumann's point in quite that way. It is true that we have a speed of light barrier on both travel and communication, but it is not true that this is getting in the way of colonizing the galaxy or spreading throughout the galaxy. The galaxy is big, but it's not nearly as big in light-years as the age of the universe in years. In fact, the size of the galaxy, it depends on... The galaxy doesn't have a sharp edge, so you can debate how big the galaxy is, but the typical scale is tens of thousands of light-years in linear size. So the universe is billions of years old. And you can say, well, it's hard to travel near the speed of light, but maybe that would be hard even if the speed of light were not a speed limit. It's still hard to build giant rocket engines or whatever it is.
0:32:34.5 SC: So to make it easier for you or more acceptable, maybe you say, okay, well, people in advanced civilizations can build rocket ships that can go 1% the speed of light. And if you have a 10,000 light-year sized galaxy and you go 1% the speed of light, okay, it takes you 10 million years to get across the galaxy. And even if you say it takes time for civilizations to evolve and whatever, 10 million years is nothing. It's just nothing compared to the age of stars and solar systems and things like that. Even life on Earth started 4 billion years ago, right? So it's not really a barrier. Like that's... I think, that was Fermi's point. I don't know whether von Neumann said it or not. But even moving at a relatively slow pace, even if you stop... It's more likely, rather than saying that you move at 1% the speed of light, it's more likely that you move at almost the speed of light in a realistic rocket ship, but then you stop and build some settlement on a planet or whatever and then you move on. Still, it wouldn't take billions and billions of years to fill the galaxy if that was what was going on.
0:33:44.9 SC: But okay, putting that aside to Jeffrey's question, I'm not sure that it makes a big difference that there's a speed of light barrier. We're not building spaceships that go anywhere close to the speed of light, right? So it's a little bit science-fictiony to think that, oh, that's what's holding me back. Like if it weren't for special relativity, I'd be flying across the galaxy by now, right? I mean, there's other barriers out there. I think it's fine. It doesn't really... My personal preferences are not relevant to there being an ability to go faster than light or not. I think that the more you dig into how physics works, the existence of some kind of speed limit does play a role, whether it's the speed of light or not. But the fact that if I poke the universe right here, the influence of that poke does not spread throughout all of spacetime instantly is important to how things work.
0:34:41.0 SC: I'm not worried about people hacking our technology. I think that that's a little bit harder than people make it out to be. And who knows? By the time we human beings do have the ability to travel to distant stars within our galaxy, maybe we'll just be a different kind of species than we are now, whether biologically or even just morally, right? Maybe we won't want to live on other planets that might someday develop life. Maybe we'll just build habitats out in interstellar space or interplanetary space around some star, using materials from planets that have no chance ever of developing life. I don't know. And I don't know whether the other species would feel similarly to that or not. So I don't think that anyone ever will design faster-than-light travel, and it doesn't really either bother me nor give me a sense of relief one way or the other.

So hopefully that thought is, you know, both important and optimistic. I don't know whether it's optimistic or not. Democracy trundles on. It's gonna live to fight another day anyway. Thanks as always for supporting the Mindscape podcast. I will talk to you next time.

segments.answerText: Hello everyone, and welcome to the November 2026 Ask Me Anything edition of the Mindscape Podcast. I'm your host, Sean Carroll. As you're listening to this, we have had an election in the United States, November 2026, a midterm election. The questions in this month's AMA don't involve that election, mostly because they came in before the election happened, but I'm recording it after the election happened. For those of you 500 years from now who don't know what we're talking about, the Democratic Party, which was not in power, gained a huge amount of power. In particular, they won majorities in both the Senate and the House of Representatives in Congress. Still don't have the presidency, of course; there was not a presidential election. Still don't have the Supreme Court. Supreme Court is supposed to be completely apolitical, but that is hilariously untrue. The Supreme Court is very political and very much on the conservative side these days. But they did, the Democrats, gain both houses of Congress. We're not gonna go into details about the election results, except to mention a structural feature that is kind of amusing. This election had a couple of very explicit examples of what is known as a dummymander. Again, for those of you who aren't following US politics or don't know how things work, there's this idea called a gerrymander, which is when you have certain conditions in place, namely number one, you have winner-take-all voting system. First-past-the-post, it's sometimes called. So in any one geographic district, or any one district in general, whoever just gets the most votes wins. Secondly, you have geographic districts, so you have boundaries drawn in literal two-dimensional maps that determine what district is being represented by somebody. And then third, you have the ability to draw these maps put in the hands of perhaps partisan governments. So if you're already in the majority, if you're in control of some state, you can under certain circumstances draw the maps however you want to decide what counts as a certain congressional district. All of these features, majority vote, geographic districts, putting the drawing of the districts in the hands of a perhaps partisan majority, are bad. They're not good features of a working government, but some of these things get in there, and once they're in there, they're very hard to get rid of. So we have all these in many places in the United States, and that opens the door to what is called gerrymandering. We actually talked about gerrymandering here on the podcast from a mathematical point of view with Jordan Ellenberg quite a while ago. How well can you do it? How can you avoid doing it? How can you look at a map and know whether or not it's been gerrymandered or not? So the idea of gerrymandering is the following. Imagine you have some number of districts, 10 districts in a state, and imagine that 50% of the voters typically are one party and 50% are the other. You'd expect that on average, of those 10 districts, five of them would end up being represented by one party and the other five by the other party. But what you can do is you can use the kind of detailed demographic information that people now have to carefully draw the districts so that the party that is not in power gets put in a small number of districts where almost all their voters are. So you could have, you know, two districts with a huge number of Party A, and then eight districts with a small majority for Party B. So that even though in population terms it's 50-50 Party A, Party B, in majority in the district terms, Party B is now way ahead. Okay, that's a gerrymander, because these districts that end up doing that end up looking very complicated. And Elbridge Gerry was the politician who became notable for doing it, and one of the districts that he drew, or I forget whether he was the one who drew them or was voted into it, but it sort of looked like a salamander in the eyes of a political cartoonist. Anyway, the dummymander is people aren't actually stuck forever voting for one party or the other. They can change their minds. And in a midterm election, which is very often pushing against the party in power, people just don't like the party in power. That's a very standard feature of democracies. So it can be the case that even though overall, usually on average it's 50-50, maybe in this election, there's a strong majority of people voting for Party A over Party B. And what you've done is arrange it so that your party has a majority usually in most districts, but that majority is small. So if there's sort of a wave election that pushes many people to the other party, suddenly you can actually have fewer seats than you think you deserved, because in the districts that you tried to make 60-40, they're actually majority the other way. This is called the dummymander. And there's evidence that precisely this happened in various cases in this year's election, which, of course, is bringing some guilty pleasure to the party that benefits from this, some sadness to the party that loses. But it's certainly an advertisement for trying to do better when organizing your political system so that things like this should just never happen in the first place. And that's where I come out here. Anyway, we're not talking about that during the AMA, but I thought it was something to bring up because we're still very much in the period of time where we're dealing with the implications of these new election results, pro and con, people reacting in different ways. It's kind of amusing from a spectator's point of view. Thanks as always to the folks who support these Ask Me Anything episodes. Those are the folks who pledge on Patreon. That could be you. You could go to patreon.com/seanmcarroll. And these days we've switched over Patreon's way of paying things, so you pay by the month, not by the episode, but it's essentially the same thing. And if you think you get a dollar or two of pleasure or reward from a typical Mindscape episode, we would love it if you pledged that much support. And as a benefit, you get ad-free versions of the podcast. Unless you like the ads—you're still allowed to listen to the ads, I suppose. And you also get the right to ask these Ask Me Anything questions.

segments.questionText: If you could have a superpower, what would it be? Flight, super strength, super speed, teleportation, telekinesis, et cetera.
segments.answerText: Classic question. Mostly a classic question when you're 15 years old. But that's okay. We all have the inner 15-year-old who really cares about these things. My standard answer would be teleportation. Teleportation. But this is an old person's answer. Okay? It's just a pain to have to travel in these awkward ways. Just last week, as I'm recording this, I zipped down very quickly to Santa Fe to visit the Santa Fe Institute, where we were having a small workshop on timelessness. At SFI, I have been serving on a small committee that's been organizing a series of events about time and the arrow of time and things like that. And this was sort of the last event in that series that's been going on for years. And so I felt I had to go. I had an obligation to go. Of course, it's fun to go. I don't really have time to go, but it was on timelessness, which is a certain delicious irony. So I went. And the point of it is, I was trying very hard to get there in a hurry to sort of miss the fewest classes that I'm supposed to be teaching while also making it for as much of the meeting as I could. And I came very, very close to missing a connection while I was flying out there. In fact, I came very close to missing connections both ways, flying out there and flying back, because I was flying directly to Santa Fe. Sorry, the word directly is wrong there. I was flying to Santa Fe rather than to Albuquerque, which is where I usually go. Usually you go to Albuquerque, rent a car, drive an hour to Santa Fe. That's perfectly convenient. And there's a lot more flights to Albuquerque than there are to the tiny little Santa Fe airport. But I wanted to get there in a hurry, so I flew to Santa Fe, which means there's no direct flights from Baltimore. And what that meant was that I was sitting in O'Hare working on my talk, as one does, and they switched the gate on me. And I never noticed until very late. Anyway, I did notice in time. So I got to the correct gate, which is in a completely different, not terminal, but region of the terminal. And so that was a close call. And again, irony, because I was going to a workshop on timelessness and the existence of time was very important. And then likewise, when I came back, there was rain or snow or something. It couldn't have been snow. It must have been rain and fog in Denver, which delayed my flight into Denver, but not my flight out. So once again, I came very close to missing that. So anyway, the point is, with teleportation, presumably, I'd be able to avoid all that, right? I could just walk out the door and be in Santa Fe instantly later. Now, there's practicalities. If I was the only person in the world who could do teleportation, then are you sure when you teleport somewhere that you know exactly where you're teleporting to and that there's not a person standing there and you land inside their body and explode or something like that? I think you'd have to work out a lot of the practicalities there. So maybe teleportation is less good than it seems. But if everyone could teleport, I mean, the world would be a very bad, messy place, I think. That would be good in some ways, but bad in other ways. So maybe I should grow out of my thought that having teleportation ability would be the best. Again, since I'm an old person now, I don't know if it's a superpower, but health would be a wonderful... My health is fine right now, but it doesn't last forever. And if you had these healing factors like Wolverine has, and you could just get better... I don't know, does that work for a stomach flu and things like that? I don't know. It works when you're stabbed, but I don't know what the general theory of the healing factor would be. But to bounce back from small indignities in your body would be very, very useful right now. I think, honestly, thinking about telepathy and things like that, seeing into other people's minds, I don't want anyone to see into my mind and I don't want to see into anyone else's. I think that talking is a perfectly good way of doing things. Flying was... Maybe flying is the compromise. If you could fly very quickly, I think once again, there's practicalities. It gets cold up there and there's a lot of drones flying around in the atmosphere these days. So if you had flying without the ability to heal, you might bump into a drone and hurt yourself very badly. So this superpower thing, it's less good than the comic books make it out to be. There's all sorts of things, higher order questions you need to take into account. James McBeath said, "In the September 2026 AMA, you said the eternal Schwarzschild solution..." That's the solution to Einstein's equations in general relativity for a spherically symmetric empty space distribution. "Anyway, the eternal Schwarzschild solution has all sorts of weird properties. It has not only a black hole, but has a white hole in the past out of which things can come but nothing can go in. But the Einstein-Rosen bridge and the white hole are not really thought to exist in the world. But we study them because there's a simple mathematical setup to look at first." And then James continues, "In other podcasts, you said that scientists should have the courage to accept what the math is telling them. How do you decide when to accept the math and when to assume the predictions don't really exist?" It's an excellent question and it points to a little bit of sloppiness on my part in saying things like you should accept the math. The important thing is you should accept the math... You should never accept the math in the sense that you just believe it no matter what. What I think is that you should take seriously what the math about your theory is trying to tell you to the extent that you think your theory is right and you've set up the mathematical formulation of the problem correctly. So in the case of the eternal Schwarzschild black hole, the math isn't telling you that the eternal Schwarzschild black hole exists. The eternal Schwarzschild black hole is a mathematical solution to Einstein's equation in an otherwise entirely empty universe. But we don't live in an otherwise entirely empty universe. The black holes that we care about in our universe are created from stars, right? Stars collapsing or other things that are analogous to stars. So the point is that there are absolutely black hole solutions that are relevant in the real world, but they're solutions that don't start with a white hole. They start with a star or some collection of matter and then the black hole develops over time. So the eternal Schwarzschild black hole is a mathematical solution, but not one of any physical relevance. And it's not a matter of not having the courage to accept it. It's just not an expression of the physical situation we care about. That's in contrast to the very existence of black holes, which was kind of implicit in Schwarzschild's original solution in 1917. And no one believed it. No one really paid attention. No one even figured out what it was trying to say until the 1950s and people like David Finkelstein. And also things like the Big Bang. Oh, there's a singularity at the beginning of the universe. Things like the multiverse, if you believe in Many-Worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics. Now, all of these are cases where physically realistic initial setups imply that the equations are telling you something dramatic. So there you either need to have the courage to accept what the math is telling you or you change the math. You change the theory, you believe in a different kind of theory, and that's also fine. I'm not against changing the theory if the theory doesn't seem to be leading you where you want it to. What I'm against is having a theory that you accept, having a well-formulated idea of what initial conditions are and what solutions should be relevant, and then just not choosing... Choosing not to quite accept the implications of your theory given those conditions. That's not what's going on with the eternal Schwarzschild black hole and its wormhole.

segments.questionText: As a European, I regularly have to watch with horror how the American election system creates really poor outcomes for everyone involved. But from a physics of democracy perspective, aren't you stuck somehow? The politicians who would change anything are the ones who are heavily dependent on its existence. And psychologically, most voters can probably not fathom any alternative without having lived abroad for some time. Do you see a path that would work to move to enable better outcomes without destabilizing society on a catastrophic level?
segments.answerText: I think this is a super good question. I think it's more just a democracy question and an institutional structure question than a physics of democracy question, but still an excellent question. If I can just rephrase it in much more general terms, we had a period here in the United States 250 years ago where we were thinking about how to structure the government. This is something actually in the book, The Physics of Democracy, that I'm supposed to be working on. I mention this as a contrast. Between physics notions of emergence and coarse graining versus political notions of emergence and coarse graining. So part of the book is saying that certain analogies or metaphors are useful. They shed light, they illuminate on what's going on in political situations. But also I try to say, okay, the following things don't work. I have a little screed in there why quantum mechanics is really not relevant to political or social situations at all. And the story of emergence and taking individuals in a large number and having them collectively work to get some goal or something like that is very similar in politics and physics. But there are important differences. And the most important difference is in physics, the correct way to coarse grain, that is to say, the particular ways in which you throw out some microscopic information to keep certain macroscopic variables, is fixed by the physical situation. It's fixed by the demand that you get a predictive theory that uses only the macroscopic variables that you've coarse grained away from the microscopic variables. In politics, you're not interested in a predictive theory. I mean, maybe you want a predictive theory of politics, that's fine. But when you're inventing a voting or representation system, the goal, the standard of success, is correctly representing the will of the people, whatever that means. And you have to decide what mechanism it is to do that. And the ability to predict the future is just not a standard for that, for the success of representing what the people want. So 250 years ago, people were debating this, and it was an interesting kind of discussion because democracy theory was still relatively primitive and young compared to where it is now. The United States in its current system of government is actually old compared to many other current systems of governments in other countries. And so they made some choices, and some choices they made were good. And some choices they made were bad. Overall, the people, though, were a fairly impressive group of people. And they were fairly thoughtful. And of course they disagreed with each other about important things, but they were trying their best to do a good job, I think. And now, as Friedrich points out, there are problems. So one issue is just this issue of winner-take-all, majority rule, right? It's a little bit different. So there's sort of two things. One is your voting system, which is to say, how do you pick the representative? But then there's also your representation system, which is what is the set of representatives that you're picking? I think to Americans, the idea that you have a geographically chosen district, like you draw a line on a map and inside is your district and outside is everything else, and one person represents that district, that's almost baked in. They don't even imagine there could be a difference from that system to something else. So they will examine ways of choosing those representatives with different voting systems. It doesn't need to be plurality votes or majority votes. It could be ranked choice voting or approval voting or there's other systems that are interesting there, but the idea that there should be a representative for a district is kind of seen as self-evident to a lot of Americans. It's not self-evident. You can do other things. You can do systems of proportional representation. If you have 60% of the people in one district members of one political party and 40% members of another one, you could have 10 representatives for that area. Maybe the area is 10 times as big as a typical US district. But okay, we can debate that. But you could have 10 people represent, and then you could have situations where rather than voting for individuals, the voters vote for a party. And if the party gets 60% of the votes in a 10-representative district, they get to pick six representatives, and the 40% party gets to pick four. Now, Americans don't like that. You tell them that, you even suggest it, and they kind of recoil, in part because they don't like political parties. And that's in part because political parties are kind of decorative in some sense in the United States. I mean, we have political parties, we split up into them, but the party apparatuses typically don't have the level of power and decision-making that they do in parliamentary systems. So anyway, this is all to say there are alternative systems, like Friedrich mentions. Many European countries use various kinds of alternative systems. These alternative systems, by the way, have their own issues. Because when you have a system, for example, like proportional representation, then, okay, what if you don't have two parties? What if you have more than two parties? It's still very possible for people to be not represented effectively, and there's different sorts of dynamics going on that get in the way. But I think... Sorry, I'm just sort of talking around the problem. The actual question Friedrich is asking is effectively, could it get changed? Could you imagine, I don't know whether for some questions you'd have to amend the Constitution to the US, for other questions you could do it just through the ordinary legislative process, but could you implement a better system? And actually, I kind of very much feel the worry that Friedrich is implying here, that I kind of don't want to upset the applecart too much because I don't have trust that the people who would do the redesign would be as smart and as civically minded as the people who did the designing 250 years ago. I do think there's no question in my mind that there are absolutely better systems than the United States has. And I don't know what the perfect system is, but in many ways, the one that we have here is obviously bad and could be improved. Do I have the faith or trust that the people in power now would effectively improve it? No, I do not. Do I have the trust that there is any mechanism that could choose people to be put in charge and, let's say, have a new Constitutional Convention that would completely from scratch rewrite the Constitution of the United States? Oh my God, no. That's a very, very frightening prospect to me. I just don't think that the people who would be chosen for that would be good people. It could be. It's possible to imagine good people really, really improving the governmental system of the United States. And by good, I don't mean on my side of the political divides. I just mean smart people who know about politics and who are motivated by what's best for the country, not what's best for their particular partisan side. I'm just not sure how we would ever make that happen. So I think that the fact that the United States Constitution allows for itself to be amended, but that amending it is difficult, I think that was a smart move on the part of the authors of the Constitution. You should be able to fix it, but it should be hard to fix it because it's too easy to break it. And even though it's clear that it could be improved, not changing it is better than making it dramatically, dramatically worse. So maybe I'm being too pessimistic there. I don't know what the real political scientists would think of that. I would love it if we had a slightly more sensible political system.

segments.questionText: Have you ever significantly changed your mind about a scientific or philosophical question without encountering new evidence, simply because you came to understand the existing arguments differently?
segments.answerText: Sure, yeah, all the time. I mean, I'm not even quite sure how to come up with an example for that, but I mean, I think it's absolutely true that as one thinks about things, one can change one's mind. In fact, I do think I'm not gonna be very good at giving you examples just because there are too many. I mean, maybe moral objectivity is an example for me. Like, I used to think years ago that you could be scientific about morality and derive principles of morality roughly based on the idea that we had evolved through natural selection to survive, and the things that would make us survive and flourish can be mapped onto moral principles. Now, just by thinking about it, and more data came in, but just by thinking about it, reading and listening to other people, I understand that that was wishful thinking. That, of course, we do evolve through natural selection, and from that we get preferences and intuitions and inclinations, but those are not morally objective facts, suppose I should say objective moral facts. They are the instincts that we get from natural selection. Those are different than what our moral principles should be. So now I'm not a moral realist anymore. But I think that more generally, there's an interesting question here about what it means to be a good Bayesian. We often mention being a good Bayesian here on Mindscape, and we cast it in terms of: you have credences over a set of propositions, and new information comes in, new data, and you update your credences based on the likelihood of getting that data. Of course, new ideas or new thoughts should count as new data. But do they count as new, how do we count them as new data? This is an excellent question that I don't know the answer to. I almost said the answer is not known, but probably someone knows the answer, or at least people have very well-thought-out opinions about these things. I am not up on the best writings or thinkings about these exact issues. In fact, now that I'm thinking about it, I have a better example. A classic example is, believe it or not, the electroweak theory. Steven Weinberg, in, I don't know, 1967, I think it was, wrote his famous paper, "A Theory of Leptons," where he showed how you could unify electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force. And no one paid any attention. It was a very short paper, appeared in Physical Review Letters. Weinberg himself didn't pay... He never sort of cited his own paper in the papers that he wrote in the years after that. And we know why. Well, we know part of the reason why. One reason why is just it was a speculative idea. But another reason why is there was a theoretical argument that said it can't work, namely that the theory seemed to be non-renormalizable, which is another way of saying that if you did calculations, you would get infinities that you can't get rid of. So it didn't seem to be physically plausible or physically promising. And then it was approximately 1972 that Gerard 't Hooft, and in part in collaboration with Tini Veltman, showed that theories of that form, with a Higgs mechanism and spontaneous symmetry breaking and things like that, are renormalizable after all. And then suddenly it became hugely popular. So five years later, it went from no one paying attention to hugely popular. No new data had appeared. All that had appeared was an improved understanding of what the theory was really about. So things like that happen all the time in science, not to mention in philosophy. And so that's an example where it's not just me changing my mind, it's the community as a whole.

segments.questionText: I love the recent episode with Greg Caruso. I know you're not a fan of free will discussions, but keep them coming. I'm curious how you would compare and contrast your compatibilist views with Greg's free will skeptic views, specifically on what changes to the US legal system should theoretically be pursued. I'm having a hard time understanding the differences between compatibilists and skeptics like Greg, and I'm hoping that when I should...
segments.answerText: Sorry, I read that without the correct pausing. "I'm having a hard time understanding the differences between compatibilists and skeptics like Greg. And I'm hoping that when applied to a specific case, like how we might modify the justice system, might make it a little more clear." Yeah, unfortunately, or for the question, but not unfortunately for the world, I don't think there is much of a difference. I think what came out in that discussion, and by the way, no free will discussions coming up anytime soon. I did Christian List and that was enough for a year, but he was on one side and I thought it was fair to have someone from the other side. And Greg is a very well-spoken and well-known articulator of the other view. So we did both of those. That's enough for a while. We can cleanse our palates now and not have more free will discussions. But I think that what came out from talking to Greg was his motivation for declining the offer to use free will vocabulary to discuss human beings making choices, which he admits human beings make choices even though they're completely physical creatures. He just doesn't want to call it free will. Why not? Well, because to him, calling it free will implies this kind of moral desert. It implies a kind of way of thinking about human beings where if you make the wrong choices, you are bad and you deserve to be punished. To me, that just doesn't follow at all. That's a separate thing. Okay. I can absolutely imagine applying the vocabulary of human beings thinking things through and making choices, making the wrong choices, or bad or evil choices, whatever you want to call them, and dealing with them in ways that do not simply involve punishing them because they're bad. That just is a non sequitur. They're separate questions. One is the question of how we analyze and talk about human behavior. The other is how we organize the justice system and our ideas of what people deserve and things like that. So I don't see any real difference. As a compatibilist, I'm completely happy with a point of view that says we should try to, number one, rehabilitate people who have behaved badly. Number two, deter them from doing further bad things. And those should be the central focuses of the justice system, not punishing people because they are bad.

segments.questionText: I was wondering whether you think it is just as well that there does not seem to be the possibility of faster-than-light travel or communication. As I think von Neumann pointed out, since our species has evolved rather late in the development of the universe, if faster-than-light travel were possible, it's likely that a species that developed earlier might have already spread through the galaxy, including Earth, and blocked the evolution of humans. Similarly, with faster-than-light communication, a more advanced civilization might be able to hack our technology and doom humanity. Given those possible dangers, do you nevertheless hope that faster-than-light travel or communication may be possible, or do you breathe a sigh of relief that it is not?
segments.answerText: So I think I wouldn't exactly characterize von Neumann's point in quite that way. It is true that we have a speed of light barrier on both travel and communication, but it is not true that this is getting in the way of colonizing the galaxy or spreading throughout the galaxy. The galaxy is big, but it's not nearly as big in light-years as the age of the universe in years. In fact, the size of the galaxy, it depends on... The galaxy doesn't have a sharp edge, so you can debate how big the galaxy is, but the typical scale is tens of thousands of light-years in linear size. So the universe is billions of years old. And you can say, well, it's hard to travel near the speed of light, but maybe that would be hard even if the speed of light were not a speed limit. It's still hard to build giant rocket engines or whatever it is. So to make it easier for you or more acceptable, maybe you say, okay, well, people in advanced civilizations can build rocket ships that can go 1% the speed of light. And if you have a 10,000 light-year sized galaxy and you go 1% the speed of light, okay, it takes you 10 million years to get across the galaxy. And even if you say it takes time for civilizations to evolve and whatever, 10 million years is nothing. It's just nothing compared to the age of stars and solar systems and things like that. Even life on Earth started 4 billion years ago, right? So it's not really a barrier. Like that's... I think, that was Fermi's point. I don't know whether von Neumann said it or not. But even moving at a relatively slow pace, even if you stop... It's more likely, rather than saying that you move at 1% the speed of light, it's more likely that you move at almost the speed of light in a realistic rocket ship, but then you stop and build some settlement on a planet or whatever and then you move on. Still, it wouldn't take billions and billions of years to fill the galaxy if that was what was going on. But okay, putting that aside to Jeffrey's question, I'm not sure that it makes a big difference that there's a speed of light barrier. We're not building spaceships that go anywhere close to the speed of light, right? So it's a little bit science-fictiony to think that, oh, that's what's holding me back. Like if it weren't for special relativity, I'd be flying across the galaxy by now, right? I mean, there's other barriers out there. I think it's fine. It doesn't really... My personal preferences are not relevant to there being an ability to go faster than light or not. I think that the more you dig into how physics works, the existence of some kind of speed limit does play a role, whether it's the speed of light or not. But the fact that if I poke the universe right here, the influence of that poke does not spread throughout all of spacetime instantly is important to how things work. I'm not worried about people hacking our technology. I think that that's a little bit harder than people make it out to be. And who knows? By the time we human beings do have the ability to travel to distant stars within our galaxy, maybe we'll just be a different kind of species than we are now, whether biologically or even just morally, right? Maybe we won't want to live on other planets that might someday develop life. Maybe we'll just build habitats out in interstellar space or interplanetary space around some star, using materials from planets that have no chance ever of developing life. I don't know. And I don't know whether the other species would feel similarly to that or not. So I don't think that anyone ever will design faster-than-light travel, and it doesn't really either bother me nor give me a sense of relief one way or the other.

segments.questionText: My question for you is as an author. Let's say, hypothetically speaking, mind you, that I own copies of a few of your books. I get to see them sitting on my shelf in all their glory every time I walk into my home office. Then one day I happen to find PDFs of those same books that fell off the back of a truck. I tried my best to chase them down to return them, but alas, I didn't even manage to get their plate. Would you be personally offended or feel wronged if I used those digital copies that were not paid for?
segments.answerText: Well, look, I don't think that the point is whether I would be personally offended or not. I am all in favor, for example, of people reading books in libraries, even though authors don't get as much money if their books are read from libraries rather than purchased at a bookstore. But I think there's an economy. This is a collective action problem, right? One person getting a book or an album or whatever, or a movie, and not paying for it is no big deal. That's not the moral problem. The problem is if you like things, if you like things that other people create and take time to do that, whether it's, again, books or music or whatever, then you want to incentivize those people to do it. Once those people are multimillionaires, the incentive might be a little bit less, but still, the basic idea is that you want to pay people for the services that they provide you, if only not for moral reasons, but because that keeps them providing those services. There's also moral reasons. I mean, I think that there is some legitimacy to saying that it makes sense morally for there to be an exchange of goods and services, et cetera. We live in this weird world where a lot of stuff is available for free, some stuff isn't. There's this whole model of advertising, right? Most, the vast majority of people who listen to this podcast do so for free, but they have to listen to ads to do it. And they will nevertheless complain about the ads, even though they're listening to a free product, and even though they also have the option of just paying for the product by going to Patreon and then not getting the ads. They will still complain about the ads. I think that people just should generally have a feeling that you pay for things that you get, and that's not bad. And of course, different people are in different circumstances. Some people can't afford to pay or whatever. The world is complicated, but I don't think that there's any moral rectitude in taking stuff for free that you should be paying for. Of course, that's not to say that various corporations or whatever don't try to bleed you dry, and that's bad, and you can talk about that. But the general idea of an economy of goods and services where people pay for what they get, I think is perfectly good.

segments.questionText: I'm having trouble thinking through the differences between an infinite universe that may or may not be repeating and a continuous universe that just bubbles off from itself. Is there an intuitive way to think about these distinctions?
segments.answerText: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by a continuous universe that just bubbles off from itself. There are models, including the one that I explored with Jennifer Chen, of a universe that does have what we call baby universes, child universes, that bubble off from the original ones. But the baby universes are not exact copies of the original universe. They sort of go their own way. So I think that there's a big difference between a repeating universe and a sort of ever-growing universe. Those are two different things. There's different ways to be infinite, basically. You can be infinite by simply repeating yourself over and over again. You can be infinite by constantly changing. I think that in the case of the universe or cosmology, both of those possibilities are 100% on the table. I propose theories. I have papers where I write and I sketch out some cosmological model. And sometimes people who are not scientists, professional physicists or whatever, seem to think that because I'm investigating a model, I must be advocating that it's true. I mean, it does have a certain sensibility, right? Like, why would you suggest this model if you didn't think it was true? Why would you suggest a false model? The point is that it's not true or false. We don't know. We're exploring the space of possibilities, right? So to know that something is a viable possibility is important, useful information. In the case of the most recent paper I wrote with Saakshi Dulani and Nadiia Diachenko, we have a cyclic universe that we claim does not have the Boltzmann brain problem, unlike other cyclic universes do. And we made the point that we're pointing out a loophole, that if you'd asked me before, I would have said that this kind of cyclic universe is not viable, because of the Boltzmann brain problem, we realized that under certain circumstances, it can be. That doesn't mean I think the universe goes that way. It means I think the universe might go that way. And sorry for Perry, I'm going away from the original question, but it inspired me to mention this idea that this is what we do as theoretical physicists. We propose scenarios. Like Stephen Weinberg in 1967 didn't actually think, because he proposed the electroweak theory, that it was correct necessarily. He thought it was a chance of it being correct. It turned out to be correct and one of the most important contributions in the history of theoretical physics. But you don't know, and that's okay. So likewise for the universe being infinite it might be infinite, and it might be infinite in a way that is never repeating, or it might be infinite in a way that is repeating, or it might not be infinite at all. All of those are very viable. We should be very humble when it comes to thinking about the very, very large-scale structure of the cosmos.

segments.questionText: You don't strike me as someone who is inspired by any one particular philosopher. But if you were going to teach a course on one person's philosophy, who would it be?
segments.answerText: That's a good question. You're right that I'm not inspired by any one particular philosopher. I'm not... segments.questionText: There seems to be a split opinion on OpenAI withholding their Yang-Mills existence proof from public view. Thoughts?
segments.answerText: Alexander Knuckle says, "I would love to hear your opinion about the latest Yang-Mills claims by OpenAI. I'm personally very unhappy how the results are communicated, but of course I'm very interested in learning more about rigorous definitions of Yang-Mills and the standard model. PS: How do you view the significance of the actual result, irrespective of how it was communicated?" And finally, Tyler Whitmer says, "I have a sort of meta question about the Yang-Mills OpenAI announcement. I was struck by the different ways the various constituencies engaged by OpenAI in the math and physics worlds asked for the discoveries to be handled by OpenAI. Do you have any thoughts on how you'd prefer these things to be dealt with in the future, especially if they are directly affecting an area where you're a published expert?" So for those of you who don't know, there is a famous math/physics problem, one of the Millennium Problems, about the rigorous existence of quantum Yang-Mills theory. So Yang-Mills theory is just a generalization of electromagnetism. These are what we talk about when we talk about gauge theories. If you've read Quanta and Fields, my second volume in the Biggest Ideas in the Universe series, you know what we're talking about when we're talking about Yang-Mills theories. QCD, the theory of quantum chromodynamics, is the paradigmatic example of a Yang-Mills theory. In some sense, good old electromagnetism is a Yang-Mills theory, but it's too simple, so we don't really think about that too much. In another sense, the electroweak theory we were just talking about, where you have the Higgs boson and spontaneous symmetry breaking, is also a Yang-Mills theory, but it's a more complicated kind of Yang-Mills theory, precisely because of that symmetry breaking from the Higgs boson. So that's why QCD, the strong interactions with gluons and quarks, is the paradigmatic version. It's complicated enough to be interesting, not extra complicated by symmetry breaking, et cetera. And what you find, well, there's also different versions. You can think about what Yang-Mills theory, what QCD would be like if there were no quarks, right? If there were only gluons. You still get an interesting theory because gluons interact with each other. Photons, at the simplest level, at the first approximation, photons don't interact with each other. In the real world, photons interact with each other a little tiny bit, simply because photons interact with charged particles and charged particles interact with photons back, and therefore you get virtual quantum-induced indirect interactions between photons and other photons. But putting that aside, the gluons just interact with each other directly. So there's a whole bunch of questions you can ask in this world of rigorously defining quantum field theories. And I'm not in this world, really, because this is a heavily mathematical world, and it's one where there's a bunch of results that are sort of a little mysterious. There are theorems in what is called axiomatic quantum field theory where you can prove things that are a little bit surprising, things that don't seem to line up with our informal, less rigorous understanding of quantum field theory, and therefore there are debates back and forth about whether axiomatic quantum field theory is missing something important, whether we should just forget about being rigorous and use effective field theories and stuff like this. Anyway, that's just a little bit of the background. The other point is that if you choose your parameters and your fields correctly, then we know that a theory like QCD has this property called asymptotic freedom. Asymptotic freedom means as you look at the interaction between particles, in this case gluons, as a function of energy, the idea of renormalization and the renormalization group tells you that the strength of the interaction depends on the energy of the particles when they're interacting. And asymptotic freedom means the more energetic they are when they're interacting, the less of an interaction there is. So asymptotic means higher and higher energies, freedom means less and less interaction. So there is a couple of informal, and that's very important, informal implications of the idea of asymptotic freedom. The flip side of asymptotic freedom is infrared slavery. So as you get to lower and lower energies, the particles interact more and more, so much so that they become confined.
