So the fact that you never see a gluon or a quark all by itself out there in the wild is supposed to be related to this fact that the interactions become stronger when the fields or the particles become further apart from each other. In quantum field theory, large distances means low energies. So when we talk about low energies, the interactions become strong. The interactions become strong when the two particles, two quarks or two gluons, get pulled apart from each other. So the energies become so large that it's easier to make another quark-antiquark or gluon-antigluon pair, and therefore you can never just take apart a single particle from a strongly interacting collection of particles, and that's confinement. Along with confinement, there is a related feature that there is what is called a mass gap. So if you have a single photon, a single photon has zero mass and therefore it has whatever energy you like. Its energy depends on its wavelength: longer the wavelength, lower the energy. And you can imagine, at least as a thought experiment, arbitrarily long wavelengths and therefore arbitrarily low energies. And in principle, you could go all the way to zero. You can't quite reach zero because otherwise that photon wouldn't exist if it had exactly zero energy, but you can get as close as you want. So if you think about the set of possible energies that a single photon can have, they go from just above zero to whatever you want. With gluons, it's not like that. So you ask yourself, in the theory of gluons, what is the lowest mass that a particle can have? And you might have been told that the mass of the gluon is zero, but there are no gluons all by themselves. Okay. So what we're asking is, what is the lowest mass particle that actually exists all by itself? And in QCD, well, you would have to define, do you mean QCD with quarks or without quarks? With quarks, we know there are things like protons and neutrons. There's also mesons like pions and kaons and so forth. The mesons for these purposes actually don't count because they're not stable. They're not really particles that can exist arbitrarily long all by themselves. But a proton is stable in just QCD. In the electroweak theory, it becomes more complicated, okay, but otherwise, for a very good approximation, protons are pretty darn stable. And they don't have zero mass; they have a non-zero mass. And even if you didn't have quarks, you could imagine making something like a glueball, which is a collection of gluons made up into a single particle that could exist by itself. And the idea is that its mass would not be zero. Okay. In the real world, we think that if you can make glueballs, they would also be unstable, but if you didn't have any quarks, there would probably be stable glueballs lying around. Okay, so all of that is to say, in Yang-Mills theory, there's something called a mass gap because there is a smallest possible mass; it is not zero. So the photons, electromagnetism, have no mass gap. You can get as low energy as you want. In QCD, you think that there is a mass gap. So there's confinement and a mass gap. These are the characteristics that you think are important for your quantum versions of Yang-Mills theory. But we haven't been able to show any of these things in terms of rigorous proofs. We haven't even been able to show that Yang-Mills theory exists in the sense of what particle physicists mean by that. It exists in the sense that you can write down the basic principles of the theory, but you haven't proven that it exists in the sense that those basic principles add up to a well-defined, 100% rigorously defined theory. Turns out that because quantum field theory is hard and there's infinities everywhere, there's an infinite number of degrees of freedom, proving rigorous statements is just super duper hard. So one of these big open math problems is prove rigorously that there is a quantum Yang-Mills theory that exists, and if it's true, prove that there's a mass gap, prove there's confinement, things like that. So again, I don't do that kind of thing. It's a very, very niche, specialized topic, actually, because most physicists just assume that it works and get on with their lives. It seems to work, right? There are protons all around us. We can make predictions, calculations using QCD for things that happen at the Large Hadron Collider or wherever; they come out matching the observations. So this sort of mathematically rigorous level proving that the theory works is of less immediate relevance to the working physicist than to mathematicians. Still interesting and important, don't get me wrong. I'm just explaining that even though I think about theoretical physics, I don't spend a lot of time thinking about the existence or rigorous proofs involving Yang-Mills theory. So as with many interesting math problems recently, in the past couple weeks and months, there have been AI-assisted proofs. OpenAI in particular, as a company, has devoted some millions of dollars to throwing CPU cycles at proving mathematical questions one way or the other. And one of these, apparently, is the existence of Yang-Mills theory, a big, very, very important problem for mathematical physics. Okay, so that's the background. The extra bit of background is, as I understand, 'cause I've not followed it super duper closely, so anyone can correct me if I've gotten it a little bit wrong here. But the basic idea is OpenAI says they've proven it, and they say there is a verification of the proof. And what that means is you can write down the proof step by step and have it checked by a computer so you don't think you've made any mistakes. That's what people mean when they say they have a Lean verification. That doesn't mean they have a skinny verification; it means that there's a program called Lean that can check the logical consistency of your mathematical proofs. And so they say they've not only proven it, but that it's been checked by Lean, which means it's correct. Okay, but there's one thing to say that, there's one thing even for it to be true, there's yet another thing to understand what is going on. And that both means understanding as human beings what were the important missing steps that this computer used that the human beings who've been trying to prove this didn't do. What are the important conceptual moves that were necessary to getting this result? But also, are we sure that the result is correct even if it's been checked by the computer? All the computer can check is that the conclusions follow from the assumptions. Are you sure that the assumptions you put in are the ones that we care about and the ones that we would consider to be the right ones? And so what OpenAI did is rather than just releasing the proof to the world on some webpage or whatever, they assembled a small group of very, very high-level smart physicists led by David Gross, my former boss, Nobel Prize winner at KITP in Santa Barbara. And he had another bunch of people who were working with them, and they were given the proof. And as I understand it, they're gonna go through it, try to understand it, and then try to explain it to the rest of the world. And meanwhile, the rest of the world doesn't get to look at it. So if that is correct, if my understanding that far is correct, I see no problem whatsoever with this. In fact, I think it's kind of absurd to think that there's any problem with this. Look, if I do get a result as a theoretical physicist and it's in a file that I've typed up on my computer, I'm under no obligation to immediately release it to the world. In fact, I don't immediately release it to the world. I write a paper about it, I think about it, I decide what the implications are, what the best way to present it, and make figures and cite people and stuff like that. And that's what these human beings are doing. That seems 100% valid and, in fact, 100% morally right to me, as far as I can tell. I might be missing something; I might not know about some sketchiness going on there in the background. But to me, the idea that human beings are given access to the proof, they're now collaborators on the project, and they are trying to make sense of it and will explain it to everybody, that's just how science works. That's a completely everyday, conventional way of doing things. Now, we'll see how this plays out, and we'll see how it plays out in the future, et cetera. But I think that we're still not in any equilibrium phase in terms of how we balance what the AIs are able to do and what human scientists and mathematicians care about. That's something that's still very much in flux. This is an experiment in trying to figure out how to do that correctly. And look, I'm not a fan of OpenAI. I think I can criticize what they do for a lot of different things. This does not seem to be one of those times that I see anything going wrong.

segments.questionText: My son is a junior in high school and has expressed interest in pursuing a career in physics. I have an engineering background and have practical advice for him if he wanted to pursue engineering, but I'm curious what advice you have for a high school student that is considering physics.
segments.answerText: Yeah, so I'm asked questions like this all the time. I think I'm just gonna... I'm probably repeating myself. I don't remember what I said and what I don't. The simplest thing to say is it's very hard to give advice because everyone's situation is different. What is your son good at? What does he care about? What does he want to be? What kind of physics might he want to do? I do think that I feel comfortable saying that pursuing physics is generally good if you're interested in it. It may or may not lead to a career doing physics, but knowing physics and studying it and sort of tackling all the abstract difficulties of it is a worthwhile pursuit. So there's no reason to say, "Oh, no, don't do that. You're wasting your time." Even if you end up doing something else, the training is extremely valuable. In terms of him getting ahead, there are debates about whether you should sort of study things by yourself before you get to them in your regular educational curriculum. I'm a big fan of doing that. By all means, study things by yourself, especially nowadays when there's so many resources online. There's online courses and lecture notes and whatever. I don't see any reason to wait. When I was taking calculus in high school, our calculus teacher said, "Don't study anything that I haven't taught you because you'll learn it wrongly." I think that was just terrible advice. I think exactly the opposite of that. In terms of preparation, learn about math, learn about physics. It's hard when you're in high school to learn sort of interesting physics, right? You don't have the mathematical tools to learn the kind of physics that physicists do at a research level on an everyday basis. You're stuck doing like inclined planes and classical mechanics and things like that. That's fine. There's a certain amount of patience that is absolutely useful and necessary here. A lot of people get tripped up because they want to skip right to the most interesting stuff, and you gotta put in your hours, right? You have to learn the basics, the background before you can get there. So learning math, learning calculus and geometry, these days learning something about computers. How the computers are going to be useful is different from month to month, so I have difficulty giving you advice about that. Don't let the computers do the work for you. Use the computers to teach yourself by all means, but make sure the ideas get into your head and make sure you're able to use those ideas. I know that the computers can solve an equation for you, but you need to understand, you being your son, need to understand what it means to solve an equation and how you would do it. Because one plausible future of the relationship between humans and computers in physics is that humans are mostly interested in deciding what are the interesting problems and what are the directions in which you should look for a solution, and then they team up with the computers to turn those vague ideas about directions to look for a solution into a rigorous solution or to a careful solution. So working with the computers, both AI and not AI, but just computers very generally, is absolutely part of the skill set. Otherwise, you gotta go to college, so apply to college. I'm a pretty big believer that you can do well as a physics student as an undergraduate at most colleges. I think that people worry too much about getting to the absolute best places as an undergraduate. As a graduate student, the total number of people is much smaller. Who you're working with as your advisor is much more important. And choosing which graduate school to go to is crucially important and changes your life. When you're an undergraduate, as long as you're at a place that is big enough that they have enough resources, you cannot possibly take advantage of all the resources as a student there for four years studying as an undergraduate. So it's much more in your hands as the student than it depends on where you go to school. You can absolutely get a world-class physics education going to a big university, state school, right? Penn State or the University of Texas or whatever. You need to do it. It's really in your hands. If you go to a small liberal arts school, that can be a wonderfully useful and impactful experience in terms of becoming a good human being. It's not as good, I just have to be super honest here, even though it breaks my heart, it's not as good for being a great physicist. Because the definition of a small liberal arts school is that there's no graduate school there. So you can get a very good undergraduate education, but you can't dip into more advanced topics. You can't talk to grad students and postdocs, you can't see the professors doing research with grad students and postdocs, et cetera. There's a whole part of the experience that you just can't get. And as I say that, I say that as someone who was in that position. We didn't have any grad students, graduate programs in physics or astronomy or math when I was an undergraduate at Villanova. So I think that was a problem for me. I didn't get to take any advanced classes that I might have been able to take if there were graduate classes around. So that's the only thing that I would, if you want to be a research-level physicist, I would point to as something to really care about in your choice of universities. You can always overcome it. There's no yes or nos here. There's things that nudge you in one direction or another, and you have to decide how the nudges sum up for your personal situation.

segments.questionText: Do you think there may be something in Nietzsche's idea of eternal recurrence if the block universe is to be taken literally? After all, if the entire history of the universe is out there, there should be nothing to stop you experiencing your life anew after you die.
segments.answerText: I probably should have grouped this one with the previous question because I don't think that the two things follow from each other. Philip's asking an interesting question, but the block universe is just a way of saying, as far as existence is concerned, all moments of time participate in existence equally: past, present, and future. There's nothing special about the present time other than the version of you that is in this time is calling that now. That's the only thing special about it. But there's nothing in that block universe perspective or eternalism that necessarily implies any opinion about eternal or finite. You can have a block universe that goes forever. You can have a block universe that is finite. You can have a block universe that goes in cycles. You can have a block universe that goes without cycles. All of those are possible. So I don't think there's any necessary connection there. The other thing I just want to warn, and I've warned many, many times, you shouldn't say things like "nothing to stop you experiencing your life anew after you die." You are a collection of particles in this particular region of spacetime, okay? That's who you are. If there happens to be at some future or some faraway, distant part of the multiverse, or distantly in the past, another collection of particles that is very, very similar to the you that is listening to this podcast right now, that's great, but it's not you. Because you're here, okay? That is another person who just happens to share a lot of characteristics with you, but it's not you experiencing your life again in any sense whatsoever.

segments.questionText: Would anthropic reasoning mean we should favor, with Fermi paradox explanations, ones that maximize the number of intelligent species out there who are capable of wondering about the Fermi paradox?
segments.answerText: Well, people argue about the anthropic principle, so I'm not gonna say what the consensus is because I don't know what it is. My own view of the anthropic principle is that what it can do is to say that given who you are, okay, given what you know about your location in the universe and what you see around you and how you reconstruct your environment, all that stuff, it's fair to ask, given different cosmological models that you're trying to say, what should my credences be in these different versions of a theory of the universe? You should update them as a good Bayesian by the likelihood that at least one version of you with your knowledge and your environment and all that stuff would exist in this universe. If there are a million versions exactly the same or indistinguishable from each other, you don't get any benefit for that. You don't know which one of those you are. You can go on to ask what are the probabilities that I'm different versions of these people who are indistinguishable from me, so I don't think you get like a million times more probability just because there's a million more observers. I do think that you get extra probability or extra credence depending on the probability that at least one version of you exists. Now, the easiest and cheapest way for there to be a probability of there being at least one person like you is for there to be many, many, many people or many, many close calls in the universe. So I do think it's absolutely legit to have some boost to bigger universes, larger cosmologies over smaller ones, but not an absolute boost to an infinite number of observers over a finite number of ones. And having said all of that, I can easily imagine scenarios where in, let's say, the observable universe around us now, which has a few hundred billion galaxies, it's completely possible that we are the only intelligent species. And yet the number of regions like ours, observable universes the size of ours, is 10 to the 10 to the 10 to the 10, in which case there'd be lots of people like you, but only one in each person's observable universe. So I'm not quite sure that it necessarily has any connection to the Fermi paradox, although there's sort of an indirect connection you could think about.

segments.questionText: If big wormholes à la Star Trek were real, what would be the safest way to enter them? In media, wormholes act like objects on a 2D plane and spacetime bends inward perpendicular to that plane. The spaceship then enters from a direction, sorry, perpendicular to the plane, right in the middle of the curvature. But in real life, they would be spherical and spaceships could not enter at an angle perpendicular to the plane. So could one enter from any direction? It's science fiction, so maybe anything goes.
segments.answerText: No, I think you're basically on the right track. A wormhole would be like a spherical region of space that had the property that when you look into it, you're seeing another spherical region of space on the other side, okay? So you're seeing a 360-degree view of a different part of the universe from the 360 degrees around the sphere you're looking at. And the sphere is not like a hard surface that you bump into; it's a tunnel, okay? So you literally just see the stars that would be on the other side of the sphere or whatever. So it's easy to imagine that a wormhole could be out there and be almost invisible, right? If the other end of the wormhole were in a region of spacetime that didn't have a lot of stars around it, it would just look black. You wouldn't even see anything. It would not be like the glowy thing. This, by the way, was one point of contention when they were making the movie Interstellar. Kip Thorne, who played a big role in the movie, tried to make them understand that wormholes would look a certain way. And the movie makers said, "Look, I know, but people have heard of wormholes before. They have a certain set of expectations, and if we completely violate those expectations, they're not gonna be happy." So there was some compromise on trying to make the wormhole look wormhole-like and yet be physically realistic. But basically, it's a sphere, and you can enter the spherical region in any direction you want. If you enter it glancingly, then you come out the other side glancingly. That's all that really happens.

segments.questionText: a priority question. I forget if I've already said this, but priority questions, you get a priority question once per your lifetime as a Patreon supporter, and I'll do my best to answer it because usually we get too many questions for me to answer all of them. So Tom's question is, "Apologies in advance because I know you don't like questions about free will. It seems that many people in this debate, for example, your recent guest Greg Caruso, try to eat their cake and have it too. They acknowledge someone's lack of free will when they make a bad decision, like committing a crime, then assume others have free will when deciding how to feel or respond. It seems the practical, logically consistent position is to treat everyone as if they have something resembling libertarian free will. What do you think?
segments.answerText: " Well, I think a couple of things. Greg Caruso, I shouldn't speak for him. I know people want me to explain the arguments put forward by my podcast guests, but I do that very reluctantly because hopefully their arguments are non-trivial and I shouldn't be the person repeating them. But I think Greg would say he doesn't believe in free will for anyone, making good decisions or bad decisions. A lot of his motivation for not believing in free will is that when people make bad decisions, he doesn't want them to be thought of as morally lesser, and therefore deserving of punishment or something like that. So I think that he's logically consistent. I think that he treats everyone the same; he just doesn't believe in free will. There's another logically consistent position, which is treating everyone as they have free will. Now, you say "something resembling libertarian free will." That makes me a little nervous. I'm not quite sure what that means. What does it mean to resemble libertarian free will? Libertarian free will, remember, is precisely when you think that your actions are not only incompletely specified and unpredictable at some higher emergent macroscopic level, but truly independent of even the microscopic laws of physics. A libertarian about free will believes that even Laplace's demon couldn't predict what you were going to do next, or even probabilistically given quantum mechanics or anything like that. So I'm not sure what use or what role the word "libertarian" is playing in your sentence. I do think that it's consistent and logical to treat everyone as if they have something resembling free will. And honestly, like I said, I don't care if people don't want to use that terminology, as long as they treat people as rational decision-making agents, that's fine with me. I certainly would not say that they resemble having libertarian free will.

segments.questionText: How does a Boltzmann brain continue to survive? And if it can't, why isn't ongoing experiences in the moments of now insufficient to prove I am not one? In other words, if I can have false past memories, can I also have false ongoing experiences or the illusion thereof?
segments.answerText: So I will say what I always say when it comes to Boltzmann brains: brains are not the issue. The idea of the Boltzmann fluctuation is that you tell me what it is you want to wait for to exist in the universe. Maybe it's a brain. Maybe it's a person who lives a hundred years. Maybe it's a whole solar system that lasts 4 billion years. I don't care. Whatever it is, in a randomly fluctuating universe, that thing will most often arise as a random fluctuation, not as a sensibly thermodynamic, rigorous evolution from an initially low-entropy state like we think actually happened in our actual universe. So everything is possible. Everything that is allowed by the laws of physics can randomly, in this scenario, can randomly appear. And yeah, it could... You could have false ongoing experiences. You could also have true ongoing experiences. You could fluctuate into something that was much lower entropy than the surrounding chaos and long enough for you to live for whatever time you want and have real experiences, and they'd be perfectly valid. But in addition to that, your extrapolation before the moment that you randomly fluctuated into existence would be wrong in principle. Now, there'd be plenty of fluctuations into things that were sort of kind of brain-like, or kind of observer-like, or kind of whatever, where they didn't think that they had wrong impressions of the world. That in fact is much more likely to not be blessed with these false memories. But that's not the point. The point is that given that we're asking about people who have certain memories, the chances are overwhelmingly large that those memories randomly fluctuated into existence. So don't get hung up on the brains. When it comes to the Boltzmann brain problem, the real problem is for whatever observers you care about, they're most likely to have randomly fluctuated into existence.

segments.questionText: I have an unpopular theory, and that is that the three-point shot should be removed from the NBA. It rewards a less exciting game. Who cares how good somebody is at shooting a long shot? I would rather see some cool plays that involve strategy, great passing, getting inside, that kind of thing. I have yet to do the research, but I don't think the three-point shot actually pays off as often as people think. I feel like players miss them more often than they make them, giving up possession without making a shot that might have taken more strategy but had better odds. What are your thoughts on this topic?
segments.answerText: Well, I think so there's two different issues going here. I mean, you've definitely asked two different questions, but that's okay, we'll allow it this one time. One is what makes for the more exciting game, having a three-point shot or not. And the other is given that there is a three-point shot, what makes for the better strategy, using it or not. As far as the strategy is concerned, I think it is pretty clearly demonstrated that given the rules of the National Basketball Association as they are currently construed, shooting three-point shots is very good, is absolutely a good strategy. I mean, this was Daryl Morey, former Mindscape guest and former president of basketball operations at the Philadelphia 76ers, pioneered this approach very explicitly. Other people have sort of done versions of it, but he really made it very clear: the two best shots you can take are either a shot right next to the rim, a layup or a dunk, or a three-point shot. As you go further away from the rim, but not all the way to the three-point line, your probability of hitting the shot continuously goes down. And then what happens at the three-point line is that even though the probability of hitting the shot keeps going down, suddenly the number of points you get goes up discontinuously. So you get an extra bonus there. And Chris, I think that your intuition was absolutely shared by a large number of people in the NBA, both sort of at the level of coaching and playing in, let's say, the 1980s and '90s. They just didn't shoot a lot of three-pointers because they thought, well, number one, usually you miss. Number two, there's long rebounds and you don't get the rebound and it's just a less effective shot. But since then, people have run the numbers and that's just not true. The benefit you get from hitting the shots, for one thing, we have better shooters now, right? A good three-point shooter will be hovering around 40% of the shots going in, which is lower than the 50% for a good two-point shooter. But guess what? 0.5 times 2 is less than 0.4 times 3. So you get less points per shot for a mediocre two-point shot than for a good three-point shot. So I think that... Of course there's a lot of extra details there. Do you in fact have a lower percentage of offensive rebounds with a three-point shot than a two-point shot? And I think people have worked that out, but I don't know it myself. As far as the interestingness of the game is concerned, I do think, and in fact Daryl Morey has said, that there are too many three-point shots. I mean, he's interested in winning basketball games, so he encourages his players to shoot them, but he would prefer if the rules were changed so that the three-pointer was less dominant than it is now. I can see the arguments for that. I haven't really thought it through myself. It's completely misleading, I think, to people who are not basketball fans to suggest that there's no strategy involved in shooting three-pointers. Everyone knows, both on the offensive side and the defensive side of the ball, that a good open three-point shot is very valuable, and therefore the defense doesn't give that up to you. They will go to great lengths strategically to prevent people from getting uncontested three-pointers. And these days, the level of detail in tracking what happens on the court and converting it into data is very, very high. So we know what percentage of three-point shots are contested or uncontested or open or not open, high-percentage shots, whatever. It's a little bit more likely to hit the shot if you're in the corner of the court rather than at the near mid-court or whatever. They know all of those things. So there's a huge amount of effort that goes into scheming so that your good three-point shooter is left alone, able to shoot without a hand in their face. And you may or may not enjoy that aspect of the strategizing, but it's definitely there.

segments.questionText: If cosmic birefringence is conclusively detected, how could we distinguish observationally between a fundamental violation of Lorentz invariance, as explored in your early work, and birefringence caused by an evolving field in a Lorentz-invariant universe?
segments.answerText: So for those of you who have not been following along, cosmic birefringence is this phenomenon you can get whereby a photon traveling through space, photons have polarizations, right? Like if you have polarized sunglasses, it will let in photons that are vibrating up and down, but not right and left. And with birefringence, that direction of polarization rotates as the photon travels through space. Ordinarily, you don't expect that to happen, but various exotic physics effects can cause birefringence in the universe. One of the first was discussed in a paper that I wrote, my first ever published physics paper, with Roman Jackiw and George Field, where we were looking at a theory that violated Lorentz invariance. There was a preferred direction to the universe against which the photons interacted. Now, consistent with what I just said a little while ago, none of us thought that theory was true. In fact, we were kind of horrified by our own theory. We were not saying you should take this seriously as something that's out there. What we're saying is we have this principle called Lorentz invariance: the universe doesn't care how fast you're moving or what direction you're pointing in. But how do you know that physics actually obeys that rule? Well, you know by considering theories that are not Lorentz-invariant and then testing them experimentally. So we put forward a well-defined theory that was not Lorentz-invariant, and we showed how to test it experimentally. But it was just sort of a toy model. And indeed, it became quite a little industry for people to come up with other ways to write down theories that were not Lorentz-invariant and then test them experimentally. So it was a useful paper for that purpose. Now, later I realized that dark energy, there could be, plausibly, a rolling scalar field that fills the universe and makes it accelerate, could also lead to this kind of birefringence effect. And the same experimental results and tests that we talked about would be useful here. And in fact, the spirit of the experimental tests we suggested, but it was Marc Kamionkowski, former Mindscape guest, and his collaborators, who noticed that the cosmic microwave background would be an even better way to test it. So that credit goes to them for that. Now, so this is different, because now you have an independent motivation for caring about this new physics idea. The original idea that we suggested was really just because it was there and you can test it. Now you're explaining something different and predicting on the side as a spinoff that you get this birefringence effect. So I think it's overwhelmingly more likely that if you actually see it, it's caused by an evolving field rather than a Lorentz-violating vector field. But in fact, those two things aren't that different. You have a field that is changing with time, you take its gradient, that is to say the direction and magnitude with which it's varying, and that defines a vector. That's basically exactly the same as the theory that we looked at. It's just that the underlying dynamics are a little bit different. And neither one of those is the only way to explain cosmic birefringence. It could be birefringence that is intrinsic to the early universe, not the late universe. There's lots of different possibilities out there. So it'll be a theoretical and observational playground if any of this turns out to be verified by further observations.

segments.questionText: As one with a strong naturalistic bent, I would tend to think that someone else's supernatural experience was a hallucination or other misfiring of his brain. But I want to keep an open mind while not forgetting that it could happen to me. If I see a ghost tonight, how do I, as a maybe crazy Bayesian, decide whether I should update my priors or make an appointment with a neurologist?
segments.answerText: Well, you're clearly allowed to do both. Look, you should always update your priors. Any data that you get should constantly be causing you to sort of gradually nudge around all of your priors in many cases, but you have to... Sorry, let's back up a little bit. What are we talking about here? A good Bayesian says the probability of a theory being true given some data is proportional to two things. Number one, the prior probability that you thought that theory might have been true. And then number two, the likelihood that you would get that data if that theory were true. And so the prior probability is there, the likelihood function is also there. And so if you see a ghost, the probability of you seeing a ghost is higher on a theory where ghosts really exist than on a theory where ghosts don't exist. So you should increase your credences that ghosts exist, decrease your credence that they don't. But if your priors are so far apart already, if your prior that ghosts don't exist is 0.999999 and prior that ghosts do exist is 0.000001, that update is not going to make much difference. Okay, so don't only think about the likelihood updating, think about the actual value of the priors also. And if it happens again, then you can start updating again, and eventually, this is what a good Bayesian would do, eventually, if you get so much data that is only explained by the supernatural explanation and not by the natural one, then your credences in that explanation should become appreciable one way or another.

segments.questionText: Since learning even just a little bit about Einstein's explanation of gravity, I've always been bothered by the cartoon image of a ball on a trampoline. It makes it look like space has a down. If you agree with my frustration, is there a more preferable cartoonish image or set of images in your mind to visualize what spacetime curvature actually is?
segments.answerText: You know, I don't mind the usual cannonball or bowling ball on a trampoline or a rubber sheet or whatever. It's not supposed to be super-duper accurate. All that that is supposed to convey to you is the idea that space can be curved. So there are many ways in which that particular metaphor or analogy are not accurate. Like you say, the most obvious one is there's an up and a down. There's gravity pulling on the bowling ball to stretch the rubber sheet, and that doesn't happen in the real world. So can you do better? You can try. You can try visualizing lines in three dimensions, three-dimensional space, that are distorted or curved by the presence of a massive object. But that's not very accurate either. If you think about... Once you understand the equations, you realize that we say words like spacetime is a unification of space and time, and it's really spacetime that is curved. In fact, the reason why the Earth goes around the sun has a lot more to do with the curvature of time than the curvature of space. Curvature of time is actually not a sensible concept, but the way in which the time coordinate changes from close to the sun or some other gravitating body to far away has more to do with the path that the Earth travels on. So no visualization of the curvature of space all by itself is going to be able to do the job. That's okay. Very often I get asked the more general question, like how do you visualize this or that particular difficult concept? And different people have different visual things in their head. They have lines or curves or shapes or whatever. They have three-dimensional vector spaces, and those stand in for 10 to the 10 to the 10-dimensional vector spaces. But ultimately, the visualizations are not the point. Understanding the concepts and the equations behind them is the point. That's why I wrote Space, Time, and Motion, so that if you care about understanding the equations, you can get those. Sadly, the world is more rich and large and multifaceted than our visualization capacities are really up to.

segments.questionText: The prevailing cultural narrative around AI is one of inevitability and runaway proliferation. However, this chain of reasoning never seems to reckon with the planetary boundaries of finite material resources and energy. On what timescale, if any, do you foresee the proliferation and diffusion of AI to become constrained by such limits?
segments.answerText: Well, look, I'm not sure that is the prevailing cultural narrative. I think that there may not be a prevailing cultural narrative. Different little subcultures have their own narratives, and it depends on which one you're embedded in. But also, again, I'm not sure I mind this runaway proliferation kind of talk as a possible future. I'm not saying that I think it's the likely future, but that talk has to be understood in a certain way. When people talk about exponential growth of anything, they're never being perfectly accurate. Unless you're literally talking about the universe itself, nothing grows exponentially with an unbounded time horizon because there are bounds, there are finite numbers of resources. So if you have the famous S-shaped curve, the sigmoid curve, that is flat and then it starts going up and then it turns over and it's flat again. So that's an approach from one kind of steady-state equilibrium phase to a different steady-state equilibrium phase. In the beginning, at the very start of that transition from the first state to the curve, it looks exponential, right? Every exponential in physical reality is probably going to really be some kind of sigmoid curve or something even more complicated than that. It's just a statement about the initial steps. So extrapolating these ideas to the wild future is not an accurate thing to do, and everyone should know that. Now, having said that, what are the limits? What are the boundaries? What are the limits that we have on resources and energy? That's hard to say. We can always just do some back-of-the-envelope calculation of how much energy we have on Earth, but maybe you're not on Earth. Maybe you're collecting energy elsewhere. So I think that there are factors and considerations that will change the future of AI before, long before we start worrying about the total amount of energy we have available here on Earth.

segments.questionText: Since you've talked about how you like the game, how would you feel if Kingdom Rush reached out for a sponsorship on the podcast?
segments.answerText: I'd be thrilled if they did that. I would love it. It's always better. I don't ever advertise things that I think are bad, but often I'm advertising things that I haven't previously experienced and I have to sort of do homework on them. So whenever I get the chance to advertise something that I'm super familiar with and love, then I'm always happy to do that. So yeah, if Kingdom Rush wants me to advertise things, if any watch companies want me to advertise things, if the Philadelphia 76ers want me to advertise season ticket plans, I am more than happy to do that.

segments.questionText: In the April 2023 AMA, you said, 'I think we need to build a lot more housing. I think it is very, very obvious that's the best way to make housing more affordable, to build more of it.' I agree, and I'm curious how you think we should go about building more housing. Should the government step in to build and maybe manage such housing? And what, if anything, would you do about existing homeowners who oppose new housing because it would decrease the value of their property?
segments.answerText: Well, so number one, I have no informed opinion about this. Whatever I say in the next few minutes, don't put a lot of credence on them. I'm not an expert on housing policy, okay? That's not just one of the things that I know a lot about. I do have experience with the kind of limitations, the constraints that are put on homeowners to do different things. When I lived in LA, which we did for a long time, we lived in a townhouse. So it was a group of six homes, and we were in this unusual situation for Los Angeles where we really had almost no outdoor space, right? No yard or even tiny porch or anything like that. And so obviously that was a thing that would have been nice to have. And we had the idea, well, maybe we could save up and put a deck on the roof, a roof deck for the townhouse. Because a flat roof, again LA, you just have a flat roof. You don't need to let the snow fall off your gabled roofs or anything like that. So we looked into it and it was just, we put money into not getting permits, but figuring out how we would be able to get the permits to do this. And eventually we gave up before we even got the permits because it was just clearly going to be too much work. So one thing we can do, that's not even building a house, that's just putting a roof deck on the house that you own. One thing we can do is just go through and make it easier to build housing responsibly. I don't mean remove all regulations and let people build housing that is dangerous or not up to code or whatever. Just grease the wheels, make it easier to do good things for society. And I think that having more housing is a good thing. Make it easier to take existing housing and renovate it and sell it. Just make it easier, because that's not obvious. That's not something that we put a lot of effort into, taking existing sets of regulations and making them just as effective but easier to navigate, right? We're not very good at that as a society or a government. Governments building housing, that's fine. I don't think it's ever the real solution to anything. I think that we want the housing market to be thriving in terms of both people building houses and people buying houses and people selling houses. A house is very often the most expensive transaction that a person ever gets involved with. Of course, many people just rent or whatever, but if you buy a house, that's a huge amount of money. And I don't think it should be that much of a huge amount of money. I think they should be less expensive. Now, like you say, there's a constituency that's against that because they don't want their current home value to go down. So number one, I don't think it's gonna go down that much no matter what we do. Number two, too bad for them. But number three, and most importantly, it's a house. It's not an investment, right? I mean, it's an investment in some technical sense, but the reason why you have it is not primarily to be an investment, it's primarily to live in it. And what happens is if you have a house and its value goes down because the entire housing market is going down, then guess what? If you sell it to buy a new house, that new house's value has also gone down. So I just don't think it's that big of a problem. I mean, unless you're someone who owns multiple houses because you're trying to get investment income from it or something like that, and then, sorry, investments are tricky and unpredictable and that's life. We have to learn how to deal with it.

segments.questionText: Your intelligence and generosity of spirit has really made an impact on me. I'm asking if you feel you received these qualities from your parents or any other influences when growing up, and if you could give a couple of examples.
segments.answerText: That's very sweet. Thank you, Alan. I appreciate the compliments. I usually don't try to read out compliments here. Sometimes they precede a question, but this one was kind of relevant to the question. And I'm not even gonna give a very good answer to the question because on the one hand, yes, I absolutely was influenced by my parents, mostly my mom. My parents got divorced very early, so it was my mom who raised my brother and me. But also other people: friends, teachers, other relatives, other grown-ups who I got to know, and also books that I read and things like that. So I kind of suspect, maybe this is not true for other people, I don't know, but for me, if I tried to associate some quality I have now with the example or influence of some particular person in the past, I probably wouldn't be doing a very accurate job. Like you could imagine that you'd put your finger on it, but I tend to think that, in fact, people are just sort of gradually influenced by many, many, many, many, many things over the years, and it's very hard to pinpoint when there was some crucial influence that made a difference. I don't think it's a matter of one person telling you one little bit of wisdom that changes your life. I think it's a matter of being in the presence of people who live well and try to be good people and implicitly picking up from the atmosphere around you that that's a good way to be. So I still try to learn from the people around me. I try to hang out with people who I admire. There's some point in your life in which you realize, no, it's actually not worth hanging out with these people who are talented or useful in one way but really bad human beings. I would rather hang out with people who are good human beings and maybe that will rub off on me.

segments.questionText: In the last AMA, when you discussed neutrino oscillations, you said something that sounded a lot like the uncertainty principle. There is no state when the neutrino has both a definitive mass and definitive flavor. I get how this can work for a single particle or field, but how does it work for three? Or is there one field for all neutrinos and the mass-flavor combinations are just different values of the field?
segments.answerText: Yeah, this is a good question. It's a little bit subtle. I'm not sure whether the answer I give is going to be clarifying or not, but I can try. If you just had a single particle, then you wouldn't have uncertainty about mass and flavor. There's only one flavor and only one mass, right? So it's not a mixture. I think the way I think about it, I'll be honest, I haven't really thought about it in terms of an uncertainty principle, and therefore I think it's not the uncertainty principle. I think there's a different thing going on because I think it would be true even classically is the point. The uncertainty principle is truly a quantum mechanical statement. It's a relationship between observables, like let's say position and momentum, and quantum states. In particular, the usual, the standard, famous, celebrated uncertainty principle is in any quantum state of a single particle, you cannot be highly localized both in position and momentum at the same time. If you define the standard deviation or the variance as delta X and delta p, then delta X times delta p has to be at least h-bar over 2. Okay. So that's a completely quantum mechanical statement. There's no classical analog to that. In the classical particle, I can and often imagine doing, telling you both the position and the momentum precisely. But for quantum mechanics, the notions of position and momentum aren't precisely defined things. They're observables that have different probability distributions of getting different answers. That's not really what's going on with the neutrinos. With the neutrinos, what matters is that they are fields, okay? That they're fundamentally neutrino fields. And even before you quantize them, you can talk about the classical fields. And fields are things that have different values in different points in space. And there are, roughly speaking, three neutrino fields, okay? I say roughly speaking because you can get into, well, do antineutrinos count differently and do different spins count differently? Forget about all that, okay? There's, for our purposes today, three different neutrino fields. And you can rotate them, so these three different neutrino fields form a vector space, which is very similar to quantum mechanics in some ways, but that's just because vector spaces are everywhere. It's not because there's any true intrinsic deep relationship there. So you can think of electron neutrino, muon neutrino, and tau neutrino as basically three axes in the three-dimensional space of the neutrino field. And any one neutrino is a vector, is represented by a vector in that three-dimensional vector space. So that means it has a component that is the electron neutrino component, a muon neutrino component, and a tau neutrino component. And then separately, there's a different set of axes, a different set of basis vectors for the three mass states of the neutrino, which are cleverly named m1, m2, and m3, okay? And the point is that the mass axes are not exactly aligned with the flavor axes. So if you are a state of definite mass, then you're not gonna be a state of definite flavor for exactly the same reasons as if I take a two-dimensional vector space with x and y coordinates and I rotate those coordinates to x-prime and y-prime, a value that is a certain value of x-prime and then zero for y-prime is gonna be a combination of the original x and the original y. So it's really just rotating vectors in field space, nothing intrinsically to do with quantum mechanics or the uncertainty principle.

segments.questionText: I'm a teaching assistant for a mechanical engineering class, and I'm pretty sure that a very large percentage of the class is using AI to do their homework, as their test scores tend to be vastly worse than their homework scores. Recently, a UC Berkeley professor made news saying they no longer see the point in grading their students' homework. Apologies if you've answered something similar before, but what are your thoughts on this? And generally, how are you adapting to teach with students knowing they'll likely use AI? It seems counterproductive to pay for college and then not learn anything.
segments.answerText: Yeah, this is something where professors are talking about this a lot right now. It's a sea change in how things get done. There were always ways to cheat on homework sets, right? You could work together in ways that the professor told you not to. You could search the internet for maybe this problem had been done before and answered. Now it's just much easier with AI to find the solutions. And so the way that I think about it is, for professors, it was always the case that their goal was to make the students learn things. And for the students, some of them had the goal of learning things, but we gotta be honest, some of them just had the goal of getting good grades because they wanted to get a job or into grad school or medical school or whatever. And the fortunate thing for the professors was that the goal of teaching them things and the goal of them getting good grades happened to line up. The best way for the students to get good grades was to learn things and therefore do well on the homeworks and the tests. So that system was sort of sensible. Nowadays we've broken that connection. If all you do is give out homeworks or take-home exams, which, by the way, before I got to Johns Hopkins, I'd never given an in-class exam before in my life. And it's not Johns Hopkins' fault, it's just I got here around the time that ChatGPT arrived. So I would give out take-home exams, and of course the students could in principle these days do those by using AI. And so you could in principle get very good grades on all those exams without actually learning anything. So therefore you have to change the way that you test people. I still give out problem sets, but the problem sets aren't worth that much of your grade. They're basically very explicitly given out in order for you to practice so that when you take the test, which is in-class, you are prepared for that. And obviously no computers in class or anything like that for the exams. And if the students... I tell the students, look, if you want to use AI to, or for that matter, if you want to collaborate and have friends help you on the problem sets, go ahead. It's your choice, because it's only 20% of your total grade. 80% of the grade is how you do on the exams. And if you're depriving yourself of the practice that you get by actually doing the problem sets yourself, then you're gonna do worse on the exams and you're not gonna get a good grade. So I'm not sure if that's feasible for everybody, depending on the class, depending on what you're doing, but it's the world. You certainly cannot rely on the fact that just because a student is in college, they're gonna do the best thing possible to try to learn things. There are reasons to go to college other than learning things. For many of us, learning things was the point, not for everybody. And you have to accept that and adapt accordingly.

segments.questionText: Am I mistaken to interpret Newton's second law to include the notion that forces cause accelerations, and to want something similarly causal in a quantum field theory worldview? Please don't make me give up on causality.
segments.answerText: So you should give up on causality, Tucker. Sorry about that. At the level of fundamental physics, causality is not there. In fact, this was the subject of a famous article and quote by Bertrand Russell, of all people, over 100 years ago. He was pointing out that causality used to be something that philosophers hung on to with great fondness, but that's just not how the world works at the level of fundamental physics. And he was talking long before quantum mechanics or quantum field theory. So some people say that quantum mechanics and the Born rule and wave function collapse undermine causality, but no, it was already not there. But that doesn't mean that all hell is breaking loose. It doesn't mean anything can happen. There are still laws of physics. It's just that the laws of physics do not take a kind of Aristotelian form. In an Aristotelian view, you might very well be tempted to say there's an acceleration and there's a force, and the force is the cause of the acceleration. But that's not what Newtonian mechanics says. Newtonian mechanics says the amount of force at any one time is equal to the mass of the object times the acceleration. Period. It doesn't say that one causes the other or anything like that. It doesn't say that force divided by acceleration causes mass. Okay? The word "cause" just doesn't appear. Sometimes in a book on relativity or quantum field theory, you will find a discussion of causality, but it's really not about causality in the usual Aristotelian sense. It's just a discussion of how signals travel inside light cones and not outside light cones. So they've repurposed the word "causality" to mean things move slower or equal to the speed of light. And all that's fine. Of course, notions that were introduced 2,500 years ago aren't necessarily gonna be the right way to talk about the world once you learn more about it. And also, of course, the notion of cause and effect is super useful and important in the macroscopic emergent world. There's a whole chapter in the new upcoming book on complexity and emergence, Volume 3 of The Biggest Ideas, where we talk about causation and we talk about Judea Pearl, former Mindscape guest, and his notion of the do-operator and its implementation in what are called Bayesian networks. So, of course there are causes and effects in the world, just like there's consciousness and free will and tables and chairs and temperatures and pressures. Okay? None of those exist at the fundamental level, but they're very real at the emergent level, and that's fine.

segments.questionText: I'm an avid Mindscape follower, and I was intrigued by your discussion with Jenann Ismael on her and her philosophical argument about why it's okay to kill cows but not humans based on their value. Value in this case being measured by one's memory of one's life, having plans for one's future, as well as these same items in others that one has influenced, et cetera. For cows, this kind of value is essentially zero, and for humans it is much greater. It occurred to me that the value of individual humans can vary over a wide range and might even be negative, e.g., in the case of a serial killer. Given that thoughtful humans do decide to kill other humans, it seems that considering the value of those that would die might be one of those considerations in evaluating the moral rightness or wrongness in making such a decision. My question is, do you think that the value of potential death victims should be one of the considerations when assessing the morality of decisions to kill them, or is there some moral or other objection to this idea?
segments.answerText: Well, yeah, I think that there's a lot going on here, and we're not gonna give the definitive answer right now. I'm not even claiming to know what the definitive answer should be. Of course, in practice, when there are situations, hopefully it never arises for you, it has never arisen for me, but when there are situations in which you are deciding whether to kill somebody or not, there are considerations about what kind of person that is. Like, is this a person who just broke into your house and is threatening to kill your family? Then you might have some considerations. Is this a person who is waiting too long to go after the light turned green in front of you on the road? That's a different set of considerations, right? So maybe your considerations are no one ever should be killed, there should be an absolute right to continued existence. And in terms of the criminal justice system, that would be my view. I do not believe in the death penalty. I don't think that people should be put to death. Mostly for me, that's a matter of practice rather than principle. I don't think that there is some metaphysical absolute right to be living. I think that it is extremely difficult to effectively figure out who doesn't deserve to be living and to carry that out. And certainly the actual government and the actual criminal justice system, I don't think is very good at that. And it's an irreversible decision, so I don't want them making it at all. So I just don't want there to be the death penalty. There are wars, and you might be against war, but maybe the other side is not against war and they invade you. What are you gonna do? You just gonna lie down, or are you gonna fight back? I'm in favor of fighting back if you get invaded. I think that we have far more wars than we should, but I'm not gonna pretend that I'm gonna have a principled moral point of view that says, "I would just never participate in a war no matter what the circumstances were." And when you do participate in a war, there's absolutely considerations of you should try not to hurt civilians. There are other people who are enemy combatants, and that's a different story. And nevertheless, they also have some rights. People have thought about this a great deal. So I do think that all of these are complicated. And more importantly, it's okay to say that it's complicated. You don't need a simple once-and-for-all rule. You can understand that these are gray areas and try to do your best.

segments.questionText: How likely do you think it is that the observable universe is such a minuscule part of the total universe that our observations are just local phenomena and say little of use about the whole?
segments.answerText: Well, I truly don't know whether our observable universe is a tiny fraction of the whole universe or is most or all of it. I'm very plausibly... I'm open to scenarios of either kind. This is, again, something I think we should be humble about. We should explore the different possibilities. I am skeptical of the worry that local phenomena allow us to say little of use about the whole. Even if the universe we see is only a tiny fraction of the whole, it's still pretty big, right? Hundreds of billions of galaxies, many millions, billions of light-years across, et cetera. And there is absolutely remarkably uniform behavior of the physical universe over this vast stretch of space and time. We can test that very quantitatively, right? We can use things like primordial nucleosynthesis and the current abundances of light elements in intergalactic space to say that things like the mass of the proton and the neutron and the charge of the electron were the same three minutes after the Big Bang as they are now to within a very tiny error bar. Likewise, those quantities and the laws of physics underlying them seem to be exactly the same in quasars billions of light-years away as they are now, et cetera., et cetera. So I think that given the uniformity of the laws that we observe in the universe that we do observe, it's perfectly reasonable to imagine that some kind of uniformity extends across the whole universe, no matter how big it is. That uniformity might not be simple. In other words, it might not just be, oh, the mass of the electron and the proton and neutron are exactly the same everywhere. Maybe that's true, maybe it's not. We have scenarios in which either one of those is correct. But even if the actual values of the parameters you measure differ from place to place, they can still be reflections of uniform underlying laws. It's just like water can be liquid or vapor or solid, right? It's just a different manifestation of the same underlying stuff. That might not be right. So it's conceivable that outside the universe we observe, there are laws or there are conditions that bear precisely no relationship to what we observe in the universe around us. But I would say, number one, there's no reason to think that. There's no empirical reason, there's no puzzle that we solve by imagining that's true. And number two, this uniformity that we do have observed gives us some credence that some kind of uniformity extends even further. So as to how big the universe is, I have no idea. As to how much we learn about it by studying the little bit that we see, I think we can learn potentially quite a bit. In fact, let me add to that a little bit. There's a very real sense in which everything that we know about the laws of physics has been learned by human beings here on Earth over the past few thousand years. So in both space and time, the extent that human beings have actually prodded the natural world is really, really, really tiny. So the fact that we can make accurate predictions about things far away in both space and time is remarkable and I think is okay to lead us to conclude that there's a good chance that there is something learnable, intelligible about the world.

segments.questionText: In mad-dog Everettian quantum mechanics, where there's a single wave function of the universe that evolves with time according to some Hamiltonian, what exactly is that Hamiltonian or where does it come from? In what I've learned so far as a beginning physics grad student, the Hamiltonian comes from some potential which is usually classical looking, or at least it's a function of space. However, in the Mad-Dog Everettian picture, I take it that space is emergent. So where does the Hamiltonian come from? Where does it live?
segments.answerText: Well, the idea is the Hamiltonian is the laws of physics. It is defining the universe. It doesn't come from anywhere else, right? This is always true in anyone's version of the complete theory of physics. There has to be a starting point. There has to be, "Okay, here's the theory," right? In Mad-Dog Everettianism, the theory is, here's the Hamiltonian, and in fact, the Hamiltonian is simply specified by a list of energy eigenvalues, the spectrum of the Hamiltonian. Why is it the way it is? I don't know. So it's completely possible to me that it just is that way. It's also possible to me that just like we only see some branches of the wave function, we only see some parts of the Hamiltonian, and maybe the parts that we see are chosen by some anthropic reasoning, right? That this is the part of the Hamiltonian where human beings can exist. I don't know, but I would deny that I need to know. At some point, asking questions like this leads you to say, "That's just the way it is."

segments.questionText: Do you believe technologies such as large language models or realistic image generation arrived at an inappropriate moment? Might humanity have benefited more from developing them only after achieving some form of enlightenment?
segments.answerText: Well, no, I don't really think that humanity is on a trajectory to enlightenment. Maybe individual humans would achieve enlightenment more frequently if they lived for a few tens of thousands of years. But we keep making new human beings, and overall, I don't see much evidence that as a species, we are achieving some form of enlightenment. In many ways, as a species, we're getting better. I'm not trying to be too curmudgeonly about it. I do think that we treat each other better now, on average, than we did a few thousand years ago, but we still treat each other very, very, very badly in some ways. Both of those statements can be true at the same time. And I think that if you're waiting for us to achieve enlightenment before developing very advanced technologies, you're gonna be disappointed. And so I don't even think that's worth waiting for. Maybe these technologies will help us achieve enlightenment or anyway get better at it than we are now.

segments.questionText: What is your position about AI successionism? The idea that if machines will become conscious, it would be ethically right to let them replace humanity?
segments.answerText: Well, I think that idea is extremely silly. I'm sorry. I do believe that AIs might become conscious. We've talked about it on the podcast. We've talked with people like Ned Block and Anil Seth who are skeptical that AIs could ever achieve consciousness, but other people like Stuart Russell, who I think believe otherwise. But why in the world would you say even if. So that's a good question all by itself. What does it mean for AIs to be conscious? Can they ever get there? What should we do if they do get there? Why in the world would you then say they should replace humans? I don't even see what the motivation for that is. I suspect, I'm not very familiar with this line of thought, so maybe I'm missing something deep, I suspect it's the usual overly anthropomorphic oversimplification of humanness or consciousness or intelligence that is endemic in certain communities that talk about AI. They act as if there's just a scale, a linear scale of intelligence or value or whatever, and we have a chance to be on top of it for the moment, but then AI is gonna pass us and then we're gonna be like puppies and kittens to the AI. I just don't think that's how it is, right? I think that whatever value human beings have morally or intrinsically or whatever, they will have just that much value even if the AIs become conscious. So it's okay to have two different species that are both conscious and can live together. I don't see any problem with that. So no one has given me any even vaguely persuasive argument in favor of something like AI successionism.

segments.questionText: I've been wondering recently about values and wanted to ask the following. Is the value of something only and always contingent on there being something or someone to value it? Or is there some intrinsic value to something separate to any human bias, preference, or valuation, et cetera.?
segments.answerText: Well, this is the kind of thing the philosophers talk about. There are value theorists. That's literally a job description. Okay, I'm not a value theorist, so I'm not here to give you the final answer. I don't want to say that values are necessarily reliant on there being someone or something to value it. I would say that values are parts of relations. They're not intrinsic to the thing. So if I have a cube of material, 1 kg of something, what is its value? Well, that depends on not only what material you have, but what other things there are in the universe that might make use of that material or might care about it. I'm not someone who thinks that value is always necessarily pragmatic. I think a work of art can be very valuable or even a little artifact that is just of sentimental value to you. Those can be valuable to you, and the value is different to you than to somebody else. I think that's fine. But it depends on the relationship to something, usually a person or something that can actually assign a value. I think the bigger lesson here or the bigger picture thing is we use words like value in our everyday life, and we know what we mean. And it's very, very common, once you get to a more careful consideration of the meanings of the words, like we do in philosophy, to realize that what we thought was a perfectly sensible concept in our everyday life doesn't serve that purpose or have that status in a more careful way of thinking about it, like free will, for example. And in those cases, I generally would like to say, in the context you're talking, think about what it is you mean. And if there's some word that you're trying to define and that definition is actually getting in the way of thinking clearly about what it is you're trying to do, then pick another word or try to talk without using that word at all.

segments.questionText: Do Feynman diagrams have ontic content or are they purely computational? I understand that all we measure are scattering amplitudes, not full histories of particle interactions that Feynman diagrams might visually imply. But it seems that among working physicists, these diagrams are essential vocabulary for discussing and visualizing processes. It makes me think that there is more to them.
segments.answerText: Well, I think this is a good question because I think the truth is in between a little bit. Certainly you shouldn't take Feynman diagrams exactly literally. And I think that's already obvious from the definition of what a Feynman diagram is. The point of a Feynman diagram is that every diagram represents one term in a sum. You add up the contributions from many, many Feynman diagrams, typically an infinite number, to get the answer to a question like, what is the probability these two particles will hit and annihilate each other or scatter in some other way? So the process, whatever it is, has some particles coming in and some particles going out, and an infinite number of Feynman diagrams that you use to calculate the likelihood of that process happening. So how in the world could we attach individual ontological content to the individual Feynman diagrams that are in the sum? It's like saying if I have the number 10, I could write that as 5+5 or 3+7. There's no one right way to decompose it in that way. And indeed, at a very down-to-earth technical way, that can be the case in Feynman diagrams. There can be different ways of calculating the same process and getting the same answer that have different sets of Feynman diagrams appearing. Now, having said that, you're also right that particle physicists talk as if they're real all the time. And that's because particle physicists are finite, calculationally bounded, rational beings, and it's helpful to think of those processes represented by the diagrams as really happening. Why is it helpful? Well, it helps you see what processes can happen and can't happen. And by doing a little bit more analysis of the individual diagrams, you can even get a rough idea for how likely something is. And sometimes you can be surprised; there can be secret cancellations. That was a big deal in the '70s when all this was being worked out. So it's helpful, but it's not the final answer. The final answer is the actual process that is going on. And of course, really the process is a process involving fields, not particles at all. So I think it's okay. Just like in quantum field theory at all, in Quanta and Fields, I try to make the point it's okay to talk about particles. Particles are not fundamental. Fields are fundamental, and particles are vibrations in them. But that's not to say you can't talk about particles. You can talk about particles if it gives you insight and helps you understand what's gonna happen. I think Feynman diagrams are exactly the same way.

segments.questionText:
David Guderian: Could you please talk about pointer states? Which aspects of them are already explained and understood by the physics community, and which aspects still await an explanation? You once mentioned that finding the classical world is still an open question in the Many-Worlds Interpretation.

Henry Jacobs: On the question of why do we never observe a superposition, is it plausible that observing always involves large systems becoming entangled with the small systems of quantum spin or whatever, and we don't consider the system observed until it has evolved into one of the eigenstates? This seems circular, but I don't know if that's a bad thing.
segments.answerText: So yeah, for Henry's question, we're gonna answer it in part by answering David's question. So the idea here of a pointer state is a state of a quantum system that basically can resist becoming additionally entangled with the world. So the classic example here is Schrödinger's cat, okay? Imagine you take the cat, you put it into a superposition of awake and asleep. The important thing is not whether the cat's asleep. The important thing is that it is a macroscopically distinguishable superposition. In particular, we're imagining here that the awake cat is up and walking around, and the asleep cat is lying down on the floor. And what happens is the photons in the box or the air molecules in the box, et cetera., bump into these two parts of the cat state differently. So they might bump into the awake cat but miss the asleep cat, or vice versa. And what that means is that the quantum state of the air molecules and the photons, et cetera., becomes entangled with the quantum state of the cat. So you have an entangled superposition of the cat awake and asleep, plus the environment, as we call it. And basically, we can call it the part of the environment that observed the cat to be awake and the part of the environment that observed the cat to be asleep. Now, nothing observed anything there, right? That is not a human conscious observer that we're talking about, but that's essentially what we mean from the Many-Worlds point of view about when a measurement occurs: when the quantum system has become entangled with its environment. But then the extra thing that is important here is that once you focus in on a single branch of the wavefunction, a branch where the cat is awake, for example, that cat still interacts with the air in the box and the photons in the box, et cetera., and the floor and whatever, but it doesn't additionally become entangled because every air molecule, let's just say in the box, interacts with the cat in the same way. When the cat was in a superposition of awake and asleep, the air molecule would interact differently with the cat depending on which part of the wavefunction we talked about. But once you're in just the awake part, every molecule either does or does not interact with the cat in exactly the same way. That's a pointer state. A pointer state is one where you can interact with the outside world without becoming additionally entangled. Pointer states are robust to being measured, to being monitored, as we say, by the environment that they're in. How well do we understand pointer states? We understand them pretty well. When I talk about the need for a better understanding of finding the classical world in Many-Worlds, I'm sort of assuming that... Well, I'm taking a step back and imagining we don't even know the laws of physics. Okay? What are... We know the laws of physics are quantum mechanical, but we might not know the specific Hamiltonian or forces or fields of the world or whatever. And I'm asking the general question: under what circumstances is there something that you would recognize as a classical limit of that situation? But if you have a world where... If you have a situation, a setup, a theoretical playground where you know the laws of physics, which is actually much more common than what I think about, so you already have the situation, you have a cat, you have a box, you have photons, you know how they interact with each other, then people like Zurek and even going back further than that, Joos and Zeh and others and Gell-Mann and Hartle, they all worked out the basic story of decoherence and how it works and therefore what states are the pointer states. So I think that's mostly understood. There's absolutely still work to be done in dotting the i's, crossing the t's, et cetera., but it's pretty much worked out. Now, to Henry's question: why do we never observe a superposition?
