So you'd have to ask the people who have trouble believing in many-worlds why they are more likely to believe in ghosts than in other universes that are predicted by the Schrödinger equation. One of the questions I get very often vis-à-vis either many-worlds or Boltzmann brains, people are like, "Why should I treat these ideas any differently than the simulation argument or being a brain in a vat or whatever, or God existing, or aliens tricking us?" And the answer is because Boltzmann brains and many-worlds are consequences of equations that we have developed for other reasons. They are predictions of theories that have been very successful for describing data. People have this very narrow and hilariously wrong idea about physics that we make measurements and we do experiments, and then all we can say is the outcome of the experiment. We can explain that theoretically, but we're not allowed to extrapolate the theory that we therefore describe, the theory that we develop in order to fit that data, beyond the data we've already collected. That's crazy. No one really actually should think that way. And the point is that things like many-worlds and things like Boltzmann brains and things like the cosmological multiverse are predicted by equations that we proposed and models and theories that we developed for other reasons. Now, you're 100% allowed to change the theory, to say, "Well, I don't like that theory." But okay, you have to change the theory. You can't just deny the conclusion of the theory but keep the theory as something you think is true. So ghosts are not like that. Ghosts are not actually predicted by any theory that we need to explain the rest of the world.

segments.questionText: You consider Boltzmann brains a serious problem for cosmology because they may vastly outnumber ordinary observers. Yet in Everettian quantum mechanics, observers on branches with arbitrarily small amplitudes are also real, and you appeal to Born rule weights rather than simply counting them. If Boltzmann brains themselves arise from rare quantum fluctuations, why can't we resolve the Boltzmann brain problem by applying an appropriate quantum measure that suppresses their contribution? What makes the quantum measure principled but an analogous cosmological measure illegitimate?
segments.answerText: That's what we do. It's the same measure, right? That's the problem. The problem is that when we do the quantum counting correctly, including the Born rule weights on all these rare quantum fluctuations, we get many more Boltzmann brains than ordinary observers. And sometimes we don't do that explicitly, but it's implicitly what goes on. If you talk about the probability at some future event that a Boltzmann brain will fluctuate into existence, that's one sort of casual, everyday way of talking about the wave function of the universe has many, many different branches, and there's a certain number of branches that have this going on. But there's many branches, and in the conditions, under the conditions where Boltzmann brains appear at all, there might be very many branches, and on each branch, there's a relatively small number of Boltzmann brains, but still more Boltzmann brains than ordinary observers. That's the calculation that is done. So, of course, you have to take into account both cosmology and quantum mechanics when you make those comparisons.

segments.questionText: In a recent article—sorry, a recent article in Aeon states, 'If panpsychism doesn't resonate with you, it's worth asking if there truly is a reason for everything, if the world is ultimately intelligible after all.' Do you think a belief in consciousness as an emergent thing invites the view that there is no reason for the universe to exist? I take it that reason is a function of consciousness, and panpsychists believe that the reason the universe exists is that consciousness exists. But I'm not sure if it's correct to think that a person who doesn't believe that consciousness is fundamental would also believe there is no reason for a universe that produced conscious beings to exist.
segments.answerText: Well, yeah, I do think that there is a relationship here. This is a psychological relationship, okay? This is not a necessary formal, logical connection, but I think that there's a psychological need that some people have to find reasons why things are true. And I think that this kind of psychological need comes very naturally from their experience in the world, right? I mean, William Lane Craig, who argues against a purely naturalistic view, doesn't want to believe that the universe can come into existence, and his argument that he gives himself is, "You don't think that a bicycle could just pop into existence, do you?" And so that's... It's very clear that he's using his experience of everyday life where bicycles do not pop into existence to therefore conclude that the universe can't, extending his experience of what happens on a day-to-day basis to the universe itself. And I think that's just a mistake. For one thing, your experience of the universe is not very comprehensive. You've only experienced a little part of it. For another thing, your experience with bicycles is part of a higher-level emergent description, okay? It's not applicable to the fundamental laws of nature, to the universe as a whole. So I'm someone who believes that things will ultimately bottom out in a set of brute facts, and we might be able to say that those brute facts are sort of natural or generic or unsurprising or whatever, but there cannot be either an infinite chain of explanations nor some ultimate necessary explanation like the theists want to have. So I'm totally willing to give up on the idea that there's a reason why the universe exists or even a reason why the universe is intelligible. There might be. Again, when I say give up, I don't mean I refuse to look for it. I mean that it might not be there, and I accept that it might not be there. So I'm willing to look for these kinds of reasons, but I'm also willing to say maybe they're not there. There are other people who are unwilling to say that, unwilling to entertain the idea that there's not a reason for it all, a reason why nature obeys laws, a reason for consciousness to exist. And people like that are very naturally driven to something like panpsychism. It sort of fits in with a worldview where consciousness and meaningfulness and understanding is sort of fundamental, right? It comes from something that cannot be reduced to other more physical-looking things.

segments.questionText: Do you have a description or definition of how or what you define as consciousness? I'm enjoying reading the many ways consciousness is currently described by others in various fields. I'd enjoy hearing your thinking on the subject. Do you align with a particular definition?
segments.answerText: Nope, I do not. I do not have a definition. I do not align with a particular one. I'm open-minded about these things. As I've often tried to say, my only strong opinion about consciousness is that it is completely compatible with the laws of physics. I see essentially zero justification for thinking that we need to change the laws of physics to account for the existence of consciousness. And I'm taking laws of physics to be very broad, the nature of reality. I don't think that consciousness is in any way fundamental. What it is, yeah, I don't know. It has something to do with awareness, with experience, things like that. My only thing is I'm happy to try to explain it in terms of physically known phenomena, not going beyond that. But then outside that, I'm very, very open to what it actually is. And I would say, I guess, one more thing, which is I'm very influenced by, remember we had Stuart Bartlett on the podcast years ago talking about lyfe, L-Y-F-E? And he and Michael Wong, who was a different episode podcast guest for different reasons, really made very clear the idea that we shouldn't put too much effort into arguing about the definition of life, L-I-F-E, because life as we know it involves a number of different characteristics, right? Reproduction and thinking and metabolism and motility and various different things. And they point out you could easily imagine systems that have some of these characteristics but not others. And so what life is is not some unified thing that we're gonna define once and for all. There might be different kinds of things that have some aspects in common with life and not others. So I think consciousness is probably like that. I think that it's a mistake to think, "Well, we've used the word consciousness for many centuries now. There must be a single unified concept out there in the world that maps onto it." I think we can figure out by doing science, by doing philosophy, et cetera., what is happening in people, in their brains, in their behaviors, in their thoughts, and figure out what is the best way to describe that. And the word consciousness might or might not turn out to be part of that best description.

segments.questionText: Could two branches on the path from a low-entropy past contain different conscious experiences but still become one branch in the future if the differences were never recorded in a way that became entangled with current observers' degrees of freedom in a way that produces lasting decoherent differences?
segments.answerText: So it is possible for different branches from a low-entropy past to eventually join back into a single branch. In fact, that is what you expect to happen when the universe reaches thermal equilibrium 10 to the 100 years from now. Okay, that's nowhere close. We're not anywhere near then. So Jonathan's question is a much shorter-term question. Could two branches of the wave function have the same observer having different conscious experiences, but those experiences don't get recorded, they don't sort of get entangled with the outside world, et cetera., and so the observer sort of comes back together? The rough answer is no. We expect that kind of thing, anything is possible, okay, but we don't expect that kind of thing to happen precisely because the way that branching happens is it's irreversible. You become entangled with the environment. That's what it means to be branching, is you have become entangled with the environment. And even if you don't write down the conscious experience you had on some notepad or whatever, it is effectively recorded in the environment. And this is what people like Zurek have talked about a lot with pointer states and decoherence and einselection and quantum Darwinism. There's a whole bunch of words that are attached to this way of thinking. So basically the definition of what it means to branch means that it goes one way and not the other way. And therefore you could imagine a quantum superposition that sort of occurs and then unoccurs, but not one that actually branches into two classical-looking things and then rejoins. The environment is just too big and the environment secretly is recording all of these different possibilities.

segments.questionText: Priority question. Can you talk a bit about Lorentz invariance in emergent spacetime? Is it a challenge to come up with quantum theories where Lorentz invariance emerges rather than is just assumed? Is it a helpful constraint on theories of emergent spacetime or not really?
segments.answerText: Well, I think this is a super important question. It's one that I don't know a lot about. In other words, so far I've been playing around with emergent spacetimes and their properties, but I've just been crossing my fingers and hoping that Lorentz invariance basically emerges. There's arguments back and forth about whether Lorentz invariance could be exact. That depends on the dimensionality of Hilbert space. Naively, Hilbert space has to be infinite-dimensional for Lorentz invariance to be exact. Lorentz invariance, sorry, for those of you who don't know, is just the statement that, as we already alluded to earlier, the universe doesn't care how fast you're moving or what direction you're pointing in. There's a symmetry in spacetime called Lorentz invariance. And if you build a theory of emergent spacetime by starting with a quantum state evolving with time, you're already picking out time as different in the formulation of the theory. That doesn't mean that the theory that you build can't be perfectly Lorentz invariant. After all, you could start with ordinary QED, quantum electrodynamics, right? That's a perfectly 100% Lorentz invariant theory. You can pick a coordinate system or a Lorentz frame, as we call it, and you can quantize the theory in that frame. So even though you pick a coordinate system to use to write your theory down, doesn't mean that the physics that you end up with can't be perfectly Lorentz invariant. However, there's also the idea that maybe physics has a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and then it might be harder, but I actually haven't really looked at it very carefully. I've sort of thought about looking at it, but never gotten around to doing it. I do think that one of the reasons it's worth doing is because we have experimental constraints on violations of Lorentz invariance. So I think that figuring out whether quantum gravity implies interesting experimental deviations from perfect Lorentz invariance would be an extremely interesting thing to do.

segments.questionText: In the late '90s, Randall and Sundrum proposed two variations of a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space model to solve the hierarchy problem of gravity's weakness relative to the other forces. What did you think of their proposals at the time, and has any further work been done on them since?
segments.answerText: Yeah, so back in the '90s, there was quite a bit of excitement about extra dimensions of space and how they could be curled up. That was an old idea, of course, but in the '90s, people started getting more interesting constructions that they could invent, basically taking advantage of the idea of branes, B-R-A-N-E-S, not Boltzmann brains. These are D-branes, typically, from string theory. And the thing about the branes is that you can easily confine all of particle physics to the location of a brane. So if you have, let's say you have five-dimensional space, but embedded in that five-dimensional space, you have a three-dimensional brane. Okay? And that's space, not spacetime. I'm giving you the dimensions of space. You could confine all the particles and all the fields that we know about to the brane, so that as far as physics was concerned, the people living on that brane would think that space is three-dimensional. The problem with that is that you can't easily confine gravity to the brane. Gravity tends to leak out. So this went in two directions once people realized this. One direction was large extra dimensions, where you could say, okay, I let gravity leak out into the brane, but gravity is weak and I don't have very good constraints on it. Therefore, maybe the extra dimensions are bigger than you think. And the most popular models had two extra dimensions that were almost as big as a millimeter in size, basically because that's where... Two reasons. Number one, that's where the experimental limits were. And number two, the numerology worked well with reconciling a Planck scale at very high energy with an electroweak scale at very low energy. You're not solving the hierarchy problem, really, but you're replacing the question of why is the Higgs mass so small with a question of why are the extra dimensions so big? The other direction that it went in is this Randall-Sundrum direction, where rather than two extra dimensions with flat space inside, they had one extra dimension with anti-de Sitter space inside, so a negatively curved spacetime. That plays very well with string theory. String theory is very happy with a negative cosmological constant, which is what you have in anti-de Sitter space. But the Randall-Sundrum construction wasn't specifically for string theory. You could have imagined it in a more general context. And they got a different kind of solution to the hierarchy problem. They related physics at one end of a very, very small extra dimension to physics at the other end, and the energy scales get changed with respect to each other because of the curvature of space in between. So this turned out to be a very phenomenologically interesting set of models, and people developed attempts to show how you could detect the existence of this extra dimension, how it would affect the spectrum of particles you might observe at the LHC, and so forth. As you know, we haven't detected any new particles at the LHC, and we haven't detected any violations of the way that gravity behaves or anything like that. So I think that it's still viable as an approach to phenomenology, but right now we're in a phase where it's just guesswork, right? We don't have any very strong phenomenological clues as to what direction to go in in terms of going beyond the Standard Model of particle physics. So you can guess things and work on them and hope they work out, and Randall-Sundrum is still very much in that bucket, I would say. Nate D. Says, "I'm a bit confused about the relevance of the various interpretations of quantum mechanics for experimental physics. Are the formalisms underneath all the interpretations so consistent as to make one's theoretical preference as an experimentalist, let's say for Many-Worlds over Pilot Wave, irrelevant? Or would believing in Many-Worlds over Pilot Wave potentially generate different experimental arrangements? Basically, this is just a question about the relationship between theory and practice in contemporary quantum mechanics." Well, we have very good limits and experimental constraints on how quantum mechanics works. So basically, if you're coming up with a new formulation of quantum mechanics, they used to be called interpretations in the old days, but I don't think that's a good way to call them; they're physically different theories, and if you're coming up with a new one, there's two options. One is you basically reproduce all of the known experimental successes of quantum mechanics, or you don't. And if you don't, you throw that theory away and move on to think about something else. So almost by construction, all of the various theories that we look at today have more or less the same predictions for quantum mechanical tests that you can actually do in the lab. That might not always be true. The theories that have objective collapse of the wave function absolutely make special new predictions for experiments, and we're trying to do them, and we haven't really completely ruled out those theories yet. I suspect they will eventually be completely ruled out. For other theories, for Copenhagen, for Pilot Wave, et cetera... I say this over and over again. I'm not sure if it really catches on with people, but the problem is that the theories are not well defined. It's perfectly clear that Copenhagen is not well defined because it doesn't tell you what a measurement is. Even pilot wave and hidden variable theories are not well defined because in modern physics we have what is called quantum field theory. And there's no consensus about how to do a version of hidden variable theories in the presence of quantum fields rather than particles. We had Tim Maudlin on the show and he talked about it a little bit, and he is someone who is optimistic about those theories, so he put an optimistic spin on it. But at the end of the day, we don't know how to do that. And hidden variable theories work very well with non-relativistic point particle quantum mechanics. They don't work very well with quantum field theories. People have tried and people have made progress in some sense, but there is no settled way of doing it. So David Wallace makes this point very firmly. He says, "Look, there's nothing to compare it to because we don't know what a hidden variable theory would say about the internal structure of a proton or something like that." So it's just very hard if you haven't developed the theory to ask what its experimental predictions are going to be.

segments.questionText: What are your thoughts on the recent elections in Serbia and the key role played by university students and members of the academic community?
segments.answerText: I have no informed thoughts about the recent elections in Serbia. The reason why I am answering the question is because I just want to, number one, encourage people in Serbia and elsewhere to keep up the good fight for liberal democracy in the world. And number two, to acknowledge that university students and members of the academic community worldwide have always played important roles in social movements. It's just an interesting fact about human life that that part of your life when you're a university student, and the students get more credit than the faculty do here, no question about that, that's a part of your life when you're exposed to new ideas, but you still have the energy and the initiative to go out and do something about them, not just to talk about them. So I'm not surprised that university students play a big role in this, and I think that that will always be the case and they should be encouraged to be allowed to do that.

segments.questionText: In general relativity, spacetime has a definite curvature at every point described by the Riemann tensor. If we measured a traveler's speed relative to this curved geometry with each point having its own curvature, wouldn't that give us an absolute standard of motion? Or do the components of the curvature tensor change with the observer's velocity in a way that keeps the principle of relativity intact? If the latter, where and how does observer's velocity enter into the equations?
segments.answerText: Well, look, you have to distinguish between two different things. One is the fundamental laws of physics and the other is how things behave in a particular situation, in a particular state. After all, here on the surface of the Earth, I can tell the difference between up and down because the Earth is beneath my feet. Up is the opposite direction. Okay? That doesn't mean that Lorentz invariance has been violated or that there is an absolute standard of rest in the underlying laws of physics. There's a standard of rest here on the Earth because I can talk about my speed relative to the Earth. Talking about the curvature tensor or any other tensor field, scalar fields, vector fields, whatever, is exactly the same way. If you have some particular configuration of matter and spacetime and whatever, you will have different ways that that configuration will be observed depending on how you're moving through space. You might be able to move through spacetime. You may be able to move in such a way that the values of the tensors remain approximately constant or something like that. And if you wanted to, you could say, "Well, that's a preferred frame of reference with respect to that field that I'm living in. But it's not a preferred frame of reference in the fundamental laws of physics." In exactly the same way, the cosmic microwave background provides a rest frame. You can say, "I'm at rest with respect to the microwave background photons," or "I am blue-shifted in one direction, red-shifted in the other direction." But that's not fundamental to the laws of physics, so we don't count it as a preferred frame of reference at the deepest level.

segments.questionText: a priority question. "In a previous AMA, you argued that the morality of painlessly killing hypothetical kittens depends on the reason, and that killing them purely for enjoyment would be morally wrong. Would you also consider it morally wrong to kill an animal for a tastier meal when a nutritionally equivalent plant-based alternative is available, since in both cases the reason for killing is enjoyment? I understand why taking pleasure in killing might be morally objectionable, but does the seemingly innocent pleasure of eating justify the killing itself?
segments.answerText: " Well, I think that there is a difference here. So I'm not gonna tell you what the right moral stance is, but in terms of what the considerations are that go into your moral stance, I do think that it's not a good analogy between killing kittens for the thrill of killing kittens and killing animals to eat them, to eat their food. Namely, that where the pleasure is coming from is in the act of killing versus the act of eating a meal. And I think that those are different. You might not think that they're sufficiently different, and you might argue that I think that the act of killing animals to have a meal from them is not morally right. I get that. That's a move you can make. But you can't say, "Well, it's just the same as strangling kittens just to get your jollies from it." Okay, this is an anonymous question. "People at AI labs appear to be freaking out that AI research looks like Go or theorem proving. AIs suck at most things, but in the narrow domains where AIs can get fast and objectively true signal on their performance, they won or lost the Go game, et cetera., AIs can run an ungodly number of trials and teach themselves to outclass humans through brute force. The bottlenecks of AI research seem to have fast and objectively true signal, like the prediction loss went up or down, and the labs are now spending billions per quarter trying to train AIs to do AI research. Should we be freaked out?" Well, I don't think that anything you said leads me to be freaked out yet. I mean, maybe we should be freaked out for various reasons, but the fact that research is going quickly by itself does not count as a reason to be freaked out. Again, I am a believer in being responsible, both at the level of the companies doing the work and at the level of the government regulating them. I do think that being careful with things we don't understand and moving slowly and testing things and making sure they're as safe as possible all makes sense. I think that safeguarding ourselves against a million minor problems is the best way to safeguard ourselves from one big problem. But the very fact that research is going quickly is not by itself a reason to be freaked out, unless you're just really upset that research is going faster than you can keep up with, which I get that too, but I don't think it's any reason to really worry at a deep level.

segments.questionText: I tell my students that the linear systems don't know when enough is enough. Is Many-Worlds the ultimate example of that aphorism, or am I missing something?
segments.answerText: So for those of you who are not big math fans out there, I think what Dennis is referring to is that a linear system is a system that just evolves in time in a linear fashion. And what that means is it never stops, right? Not only does it go at the same rate, it goes at the same rate forever. So if you had linear growth of some system, it would just keep growing forever and ever and ever. This is actually a well-known issue when people try to model mathematically things like the growth of species or environmental issues and things like that, because very often you start with some simple model that does well describing some tiny period of time, but the model just grows. It just sort of blows up and is unstable and doesn't really do a good job. So you invent non-linear effects that say, "Okay, you can grow for a little while, but if you grow too far, then a new term kicks in which kills you off and stops you from growing." That's a very, very standard move in ecological or biological modeling. So Dennis's question is, is Many-Worlds the ultimate example of this? And maybe. I think that Many-Worlds is the consequence of taking the Schrödinger equation literally at face value. And the Schrödinger equation is linear. So in that sense, yes. There is a further tricky thing, though. It does depend on the space in which you are evolving. After all, if your space of possibilities is a circle, then even if you move on the circle linearly, that is to say at a constant angular velocity, you don't go crazy. You just keep coming back to where you left again and again and again, right? Just go around the circle an infinite number of times. Nothing to be worried about there. If you're moving through a plane, a two-dimensional Euclidean plane, and you're moving in a straight line, then you will go off forever. So this is analogous in quantum mechanics to asking whether or not Hilbert space is finite-dimensional or infinite-dimensional. That's why in my recent paper, you got a cyclic universe out of a situation where you were in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, because then you evolve linearly, but you come back to where you left. That's where the cyclic universe comes from. If Hilbert space is infinite-dimensional, then you can evolve forever and ever. And Many-Worlds is basically taking advantage of that. Absolutely.

segments.questionText: Given the state of our democracy, I've been thinking about Gödel's loophole, and I'm wondering if this is the inner inconsistency he was thinking about. Do you have any thoughts on this?
segments.answerText: So I have some thoughts. I'm not sure how accurate my thoughts are. So for those of you who don't know, there's a famous story of Kurt Gödel, the logician, who moved to the United States. He was from, I think he was from Germany, but maybe Austria, I'm not sure. Anyway, he got a job at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, he became friends with Einstein, et cetera. And eventually he applied for citizenship in the United States. And there's a test you have to take to become a citizen. And one of the questions is something about democracy in the United States. And according to the story, there's different versions of it, I don't really believe any of them, but according to the story, Gödel starts saying, "Well, actually there is a way within the Constitution to overthrow the government of the United States and make it non-democratic." And some people try to wonder whether or not this is related to Gödel's formal work, his logical work in showing that there are inconsistencies that lay, possible inconsistencies or at least possible paradoxes in logical systems. But as far as I know, nobody actually knows, maybe someone does, but hasn't told me, what Gödel actually had in mind when he was thinking about this. And honestly, I know people speculate about it. I don't quite see what the big deal is. I think that this is, it's basically impossible to design a democratic system that can't be overturned for the very simple reason that if all of the people in a democracy decide to get rid of democracy, they can do it, right? That's not something you can even stop from happening no matter how you design your system. So I don't think you need to be a super-genius like Gödel was to notice that in the Constitution of the United States there are ways to amend the Constitution. And you could amend the Constitution to say that there is a dictator, right? There's an emperor, if you wanted to do that. That's 100% valid. You don't need to be very smart to figure that out. So this is something you just have to live with. I mean, this is why it's crucially important if you do want to live in a democracy, which we've been talking about before, that the populace be educated and civic-minded. You can't have a democracy of reluctant citizens or citizens that don't believe in the values of democracy, because if they don't believe in those values, they can easily get rid of the democracy. You can't force democracy on people who don't want it, no matter how hard you try. So you have to give the sales pitch for democracy. You have to let people know how important it is. And democracy is not just about giving people a voice. That's part of it. But oftentimes people say, "Well, I like democracy because I like to be able to vote. I like to have a say in the government." And what they're less enthusiastic about is other people having a say. What democracy is really about is not voting for your favorite thing, but acquiescing when the majority of people in your country vote for something different, for agreeing to go along with majority rule. And of course you want to safeguard against violating the rights of minorities, et cetera. That's why you have various checks and balances in the Constitution, and you have a republican system, and you have federalism and all these different things, and you have a Bill of Rights. Okay. So you don't want the majority to get everything at once, but for the most part you want majority rule, which means that sometimes you're gonna be in the minority and you have to learn to live with that. And I think that that is something that we don't do a good job of explaining to people so that they are willing to fight for the principle that sometimes they're not gonna get their way. Because when people fantasize about how awesome it would be to have a strongman, dictator, authoritarian, in their minds, their strongman is always on their side. And they just don't quite accept that maybe even if the strongman initially looked like they were gonna go along with their side, they can change their minds, their incentive structure might be different, and therefore it is better to just avoid the possibility of anyone having that authoritative power at all. So I don't know what Kurt was thinking about, but I don't think you need to think that hard. We do need to make sure that the democracy is solid at the level of the opinions of the actual citizens of the democracy, not just at the level of the laws that we're all supposed to be obeying. So hopefully that thought is, you know, both important and optimistic. I don't know whether it's optimistic or not. Democracy trundles on. It's gonna live to fight another day anyway. Thanks as always for supporting the Mindscape podcast. I will talk to you next time.
